title: Orlandu's Arcade — Retro Arcade Games & Sony Pro Monitors
description: A private arcade and Sony professional monitor collection in Orange County, California — arcade cabinets, pinball, RGB-modded consoles, and a Trinitron fleet.
text:
## Step inside
 Coin-Op Games

### Two Rooms of Cabinets & Pinball

The garage arcade with four uprights and the pinball row, plus the inside game room with the candy cab and cocktail — six cabinets and four pins in all.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/games.html) The Monitor Fleet

### Sony PVM · BVM · LMD

A working museum of Sony professional video — thirteen units across eight models, documented in the Trinitron Fleet magazine.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/monitors.html) The Consoles

### Nintendo · Sega · NEC · Sony

From front-loader NES to the PC Engine Duo-R and Turbo Express — the home hardware that feeds the CRTs, much of it RGB-modded or restored.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/consoles.html) The PlayChoice-10 Cart Wall

### Fifty-Two Game Boards

The whole PlayChoice-10 library as bare green boards, photographed one by one — plus ten conversions and custom builds, and what each label and code tells you.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/playchoice-10.html) The Signage Wall

### Toppers, Cards & Lit Retail Signs

Nineteen original PlayChoice-10 arcade toppers, eighteen NOS VS. instruction cards, and the Nintendo retail signage that told a shop floor what was inside.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/signage.html) The Guide Shelf

### Twenty-One Player’s Guides

Nintendo’s official strategy guides, photographed cover by cover — the SNES years, from A Link to the Past to Chrono Trigger.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/guide-shelf.html) The Spinning Top Wall

### Sixty Foreverspin Tops

One shape turned in thirty-five metals, from 6 g magnesium to 60 g tungsten, plus twenty-five mystery tops and limited editions — each photographed off its base.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/spinning-tops.html) Gallery

### Photos & Video from the Arcade

The growing photo and video log — new shots from the garage land here as they happen.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/gallery.html) Stories

### Monographs, Guides & Magazines

Twelve long reads from the collection — the AMS-100 monograph, the PVM-20L5 buying guide, Trinitron Fleet, the Orlandu 100 and 50, and more.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/stories.html) Workbench

### Current & Completed Projects

Repairs, rebuilds, and restorations — from pinball board swaps to arcade PSU rebuilds and CRT calibration.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/projects.html) For Sale

### Duplicates & Departures

The collection consolidates over time. Monitors and hardware currently listed for sale live here.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/forsale.html) Wanted

### The Hunt List

Actively searching: BKM input cards, specific consumer CRTs, and a few white whales. Have one? Get in touch.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html)

## The reading room
 Monograph

### The Sony AMS-100 Has No Written History

The primary literature on Sony’s modular audio confidence monitor — the frame, the board system, a registry of documented units, and the market record.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/ams-100-monograph.html) Magazine

### Trinitron Fleet, Vol. 1

The interactive magazine on the monitor fleet — every model with its full spec sheet, the battle of the twenties, and how to speak broadcast.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/trinitron-fleet-vol1.html) Buyer’s Guide

### What to Check Before You Buy a PVM-20L5

The geometry grid, judging a tube with no hours counter, what to pay — and why you should drive to it rather than ship it.
 (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-20l5-buying-guide.html)

## Latest from the arcade
 New

### Ask your AI assistant about the arcade

An MCP server, a full-text file and three open datasets let Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any agent search the site, read a page and query the monitor specs — no key, no scraping. How to connect it → (https://www.orlandu.com/mcp.html)
 New how-to

### Console to PVM, cable by cable

What actually plugs into what to get a retro console onto a Sony professional monitor — the RGB cable, the switcher, the SCART to 4 BNC breakout, sync, termination and audio, and the one box you do not need. Read the how-to → (https://www.orlandu.com/connect-console-to-pvm.html)
 New page

### The spinning top wall

Sixty Foreverspin tops photographed off their bases — thirty-five metals from 6 g magnesium to 60 g tungsten, plus twenty-five mystery tops and limited editions. See the wall → (https://www.orlandu.com/spinning-tops.html)
 New page

### The PlayChoice-10 cart wall

The whole PlayChoice-10 library, board by board, plus ten conversions and custom builds with the story of each — and what the bare green PCB and its two-letter code actually tell you. See the cart wall → (https://www.orlandu.com/playchoice-10.html)
 New pages

### Every monitor gets its own page

The PVM-2950Q, PVM-20L5, BVM-20E1U, BVM-A14F5U and the LMD wall each get a full profile — the feature, the inputs and cards, and the work log. Start at the roster → (https://www.orlandu.com/monitors.html)
 New page

### Forty years on one line

Every machine, console and monitor plotted by the year it was released — scroll down from the 1981 Donkey Kong to the 2020 Rick and Morty. See the timeline → (https://www.orlandu.com/timeline.html)
 Found

### Captain Skyhawk comes off the hunt list

An original 1989 PlayChoice-10 topper — Rare’s jet shooter, printed for Milton Bradley and licensed by Nintendo. See it on the topper wall → (https://www.orlandu.com/signage.html#toppers)
 Published

### The Orlandu 100

A hundred favorite films ranked by head-to-head duel — no CRTs, no coin doors, just the same instinct pointed somewhere else. Read the issue → (https://www.orlandu.com/orlandu-100.html)
 Published

### Spotting professional glass in the wild

How to tell a Sony professional monitor from a heavy old TV at a thrift store or estate sale — and what to check before you haul it home. Read the field guide → (https://www.orlandu.com/crt-field-guide.html)

title: Coin-Op Games: Arcade Cabinets & Pinball
description: Arcade cabinets, pinball machines, and the game room at Orlandu's Arcade — Donkey Kong, Mario Bros., VS. UniSystem, Indiana Jones and more.
text:
Press Start

# Coin-Op Games

Orlandu's Arcade lives in two rooms: the garage arcade — four uprights, the pinball row, and the broadcast monitor racks — and the game room inside the house, where the candy cab and the cocktail hold court.
 Uprights Pinball Game Room In Memoriam Console Library

## The garage arcade — uprights

[Photo: Nintendo Donkey Kong upright in blue plywood, marquee lit]

 Nintendo · 1981

### Donkey Kong

Blue plywood — the machine that started Nintendo's arcade legend, and most collections worth the name. The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/donkey-kong.html)

[Photo: Nintendo Mario Bros. widebody arcade cabinet, marquee lit]

 Nintendo · 1983

### Mario Bros. — Widebody

Two players, one sewer. The widebody Mario Bros. joins the Nintendo upright lineup. The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/mario-bros.html)

[Photo: Nintendo VS. UniSystem dedicated arcade cabinet with the VS. Super Mario Bros. marquee lit]

 Nintendo · 1984

### VS. UniSystem — Dedicated

Nintendo's arcade answer to the NES era. A VS. Interchanger runs both VS. Super Mario Bros. and VS. Duck Hunt — and the Mario is not the game you think it is. Did you know? → (https://www.orlandu.com/vs-smb.html) The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/vs-unisystem.html)

[Photo: Dynamo Big Blue arcade cabinet in blue with Capcom side art and a Marvel vs. Capcom marquee]

 Dynamo Gen 1 · 1992

### Big Blue

The classic American showcase cabinet — rebuilt power supply, and now wearing fresh Capcom-logo side art. It runs a Darksoft CPS-2 multi in a Jasen's Customs case, so the whole CPS-2 library is on tap — Marvel vs. Capcom most of the time. The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/big-blue.html)

## The garage arcade — pinball row

[Photo: Williams Indiana Jones widebody pinball machine, backbox lit]

 Williams · 1993

### Indiana Jones: The Pinball Adventure

The widebody DCS-era classic — three films on one playfield, and Williams’ first year of digital sound. The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/indiana-jones.html)

[Photo: Stern Ghostbusters Premium pinball machine, backbox and topper lit]

 Stern · 2016

### Ghostbusters Premium

Who you gonna call when the magna-slings throw the ball somewhere unfair? Nobody. That's the game. The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/ghostbusters.html)

[Photo: Total Nuclear Annihilation pinball machine by Spooky Pinball with its full topper set]

 Spooky Pinball · 2017

### Total Nuclear Annihilation

Scott Danesi's synthwave fever dream. Fast, brutal, single-level, perfect. The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/tna.html)

[Photo: Spooky Pinball Rick and Morty Blood Sucker Edition pinball machine, backbox lit]

 Spooky · 2020

### Rick and Morty — Blood Sucker Edition

The limited Blood Sucker Edition — bought new in box, home use only, running in its original butter cabinet. The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/rick-and-morty.html)

## The game room inside the house

[Photo: The restored Red Tent cocktail seen at an angle, VS. Excitebike on the screen and three PlayChoice-10 toppers displayed on the canopy]

 Nintendo · 1984

### VS. DualSystem — Red Tent Cocktail

The rarer sit-down side of the VS. family — the distinctive red-canopy cocktail DualSystem. The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/red-tent.html)

[Photo: The pink Capcom Mini Cute candy cabinet head on at night, Street Fighter II lit on its screen and a Capcom poster above]

 Capcom Candy Cab · 1991

### Mini Cute — Pink

The only candy-style cabinet in the collection, and it's the one that matters: Capcom's compact Mini Cute in the pink variant. The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/mini-cute.html)

The game room also hosts the big PVMs — the 29-inch PVM-2950Q and the PVM-20L5. Meet the fleet → (https://www.orlandu.com/monitors.html)

## Console library

Beyond the cabinets there's a cataloged collection of consoles and games — nearly 900 titles logged, from the NES shelf to the TurboGrafx HuCards. The hardware has its own page (https://www.orlandu.com/consoles.html), and the PlayChoice-10 game boards that ran in cabinets like the one in the memoriam above have a wall of their own (https://www.orlandu.com/playchoice-10.html) — all fifty-two Nintendo released. And if a word on these pages — JAMMA, CPO, shop-out, candy cab — went by without an explanation, the glossary (https://www.orlandu.com/glossary.html) has it. Every machine here, and every console and monitor, is also on one timeline (https://www.orlandu.com/timeline.html), in the order each was released.

title: Sony PVM, BVM & LMD Monitor Fleet
description: The Sony professional monitor fleet at Orlandu's Arcade: PVM, BVM, and LMD broadcast and production monitors, documented in the Trinitron Fleet magazine.
text:
Sony Professional Video

# The Monitor Fleet

A working museum of Sony professional displays — broadcast BVMs, production PVMs, and the LMD generation that followed. Thirteen units across eight models.
 Vol. 1

### TRINITRON FLEET — the magazine

The full story of the fleet, told properly: an interactive magazine covering every chassis, the calibration work, and why these monitors matter. Future volumes will follow as the fleet evolves.

## The fleet roster

[Photo: Sony PVM-2950Q 29-inch Trinitron production monitor lit at night running Super Mario World, its control panel and the SONY badge in frame]

 PVM · Production

### PVM-2950Q

Twenty-nine inches of presence, the biggest tube in the room. On screen: *Super Mario World*, 1990.

The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-2950q.html) · Feature in Vol. 1 → (https://www.orlandu.com/trinitron-fleet-vol1.html#f0)

[Photo: Sony PVM-20L5 multiformat Trinitron monitor lit and running Super Mario Sunshine, an AMS-100 audio monitor on top and both control strips in frame]

 PVM · Production

### PVM-20L5

The late-generation 20-inch multiformat, AMS-100 riding on top. On screen: *Super Mario Sunshine*, 2002 — the year this generation of chassis arrived, at 480p over component.

The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-20l5.html) · Feature in Vol. 1 → (https://www.orlandu.com/trinitron-fleet-vol1.html#f1)

[Photo: Sony BVM-20E1U broadcast monitor lit in its rack running Chrono Trigger, with an AMS-100 audio monitor speaker on top]

 BVM · Broadcast

### BVM-20E1U

The primary broadcast chassis, AMS-100 riding on top. On screen: *Chrono Trigger*, 1995 — the year this chassis went into production.

The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/bvm-20e1u.html) · Feature in Vol. 1 → (https://www.orlandu.com/trinitron-fleet-vol1.html#f2)

[Photo: Sony BVM-A14F5U broadcast monitor lit and running Beggar Prince on the Sega Genesis, with its full control panel and an AMS-100 speaker above]

 BVM · Broadcast

### BVM-A14F5U

Two of three card slots filled, control panel and keypad flanking the tube. On screen: *Beggar Prince*, 2006 — a brand-new Genesis game a decade after Sega walked away, on the last CRT generation Sony ever built.

The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/bvm-a14f5u.html) · Feature in Vol. 1 → (https://www.orlandu.com/trinitron-fleet-vol1.html#f3)

[Photo: Three Sony LMD professional LCD monitors side by side, all showing the same cartoon frame]

 LMD · Four models · Nine units

### The LMD wall

The flat-panel side of the fleet, and the confidence layer behind the tubes — one shared 8.4-inch chassis family, one manual, one job: keep every signal honest before it reaches glass that matters.
 **LMD-940W** · widescreen 9-inch, HDMI to 3G**LMD-9020** · the analog corner**LMD-9030 ×5** · the rack squadron**LMD-9050 ×2** · HD-SDI

The full profile → (https://www.orlandu.com/lmd-wall.html) · Feature in Vol. 1 → (https://www.orlandu.com/trinitron-fleet-vol1.html#f4)

How every one of these actually gets a signal — the switchers, the SCART-to-BNC cables, and the distribution amp behind the LMD wall — is written up in The Signal Chain (https://www.orlandu.com/signal-chain.html); the vocabulary — TVL, multiscan, BKM, loop-through — is in the glossary (https://www.orlandu.com/glossary.html). Recently departed: a BVM-14F5U and the nine-inch BVM-D9H5J found new homes — the fleet consolidates so the keepers get the attention they deserve.

 Sony AMS-100

title: Sony PVM-2950Q: Specs, Inputs & Work Log
description: The cube. Twenty-nine inches of Super Trinitron, 115 pounds, and the biggest tube Sony ever put in a production monitor.
text:
[Photo: Sony PVM-2950Q 29-inch Trinitron production monitor lit at night running Super Mario World]

***In the fleet** — PVM production*

 Monitor Profile

# Sony PVM-2950Q

The cube. Twenty-nine inches of Super Trinitron, 115 pounds, and the biggest tube Sony ever put in a production monitor.
 FamilyPVMSize29"Resolution600 TVLEra1991–1996

Every collection has a centerpiece, and this one announces itself before it is ever switched on. The PVM-2950Q is twenty-nine inches of Super Trinitron in a hundred-and-fifteen-pound cube — the biggest tube Sony ever committed to a production monitor, and the closest thing the format has to a monument.

Turn it on and the monument becomes a window. This is arcade-era spectacle at living-room scale: the same glass family the era's games were mastered against, blown up until sprites carry real physical weight. At 600 TVL the scanlines land soft and warm rather than surgical, and across a 27-inch face that is not a limitation — it is the original artistic intent, projected at full size.

Sit a 16-bit console in front of it and the effect is immediate. Color snaps. Blacks fall away to nothing. Motion arrives with zero apology. NTSC, PAL, SECAM — it auto-detects and simply gets on with the job, the way broadcast hardware always did, no menus to negotiate and nothing to configure.

And here is the quietly great part: beneath the brute scale sits the most serviceable big CRT Sony ever made. Convergence and geometry live in a digital service menu — the finest implementation in the PVM class — so keeping the picture perfect decades on is a menu exercise rather than folklore. Machines this size usually demand rituals. This one just asks for a shelf strong enough to hold it.

> Arcade-era spectacle at living-room scale — a monument that doubles as a window.

## Inputs, formats, and what it takes

- **Formats**: NTSC / PAL / SECAM / NTSC 4.43, auto-select
- **Sync**: 15 kHz only
- **Composite**: 2× with loop-through
- **Y/C**: Yes
- **RGB / component**: RGB (BNC)
- **SD-SDI**: None
- **HD-SDI**: None
- **Option slots**: None — fixed inputs
- **Control**: Front panel + OSD; full digital geometry/convergence in service menu
- **Weight**: 115 lb (52 kg, Sony spec)

## Work log

What has been done to it since it arrived.

- **SS-X7A speakers fitted** — Sony's own optional speaker pair for the 2950, hung on the cabinet the way the catalog showed them.
- **Full calibration** — Geometry and convergence walked through the digital service menu — no pots, no folklore.

- **Family**: **Sony PVM** — Super Trinitron CRT
- **Era**: **1991–1996** — Native scan, soft scanlines at 600 TVL
- **Status**: **In service** — Lit and in use, the big-screen 240p display.

## Quick answers

### What is the Sony PVM-2950Q?

Sony's 29-inch Super Trinitron production monitor, built from 1991 to 1996: 600 TV lines on a 27-inch viewable face, 115 pounds, and the biggest tube Sony ever committed to a production monitor.

### How heavy is a PVM-2950Q?

115 lb (52 kg) by Sony's own spec. Machines this size usually demand rituals; this one asks for a shelf strong enough to hold it.

### What inputs does the PVM-2950Q have?

Two composite inputs with loop-through, Y/C, and RGB on BNCs. No option slot and no SDI — the inputs are fixed. It auto-selects NTSC, PAL, SECAM and NTSC 4.43, and it is 15 kHz only: standard definition by design.

### Is the PVM-2950Q good for retro games?

It is the big-screen 240p display here. At 600 TVL the scanlines land soft and warm across the whole face, and a 16-bit console in front of it is the reason to own one. Geometry and convergence live in a digital service menu, so keeping the picture right decades on is a menu exercise rather than folklore.

More photos in the gallery → (https://www.orlandu.com/gallery.html#tag=pvm-2950q)

The long-form feature, the full 28-line spec sheet and its sources are in Trinitron Fleet, Vol. 1 (https://www.orlandu.com/trinitron-fleet-vol1.html#f0); the side-by-side of every model is on the fleet page (https://www.orlandu.com/monitors.html#specs). Vocabulary — TVL, multiscan, BKM, loop-through — is in the glossary (https://www.orlandu.com/glossary.html).

title: Sony PVM-20L5: Specs, Inputs & Work Log
description: The king of PVMs. The last and best of Sony's production line, multiscan from 240p to 1080i on 800 lines of HR Trinitron.
text:
[Photo: Sony PVM-20L5 multiformat Trinitron monitor lit and running Super Mario Sunshine, an AMS-100 on top]

***In the fleet** — PVM production (top of line)*

 Monitor Profile

# Sony PVM-20L5

The king of PVMs. The last and best of Sony's production line, multiscan from 240p to 1080i on 800 lines of HR Trinitron.
 FamilyPVM (top of line)Size20"Resolution800 TVLEra2002–2007

Ask around the hobby and one name keeps coming back. The 20L5 is the king of PVMs — full stop — the machine that arrived at the very end of Sony's production-monitor line with thirty years of Trinitron lessons folded into it. Plug anything into it, from any decade, and it shows why the title stuck.

The party trick is range. This is a true multiscan machine, locking anything from 15 to 33.75 kHz: a Super Nintendo at 240p, a DVD player at 480p, a broadcast feed at 1080i — same glass, same effortless lock, no option card required. One monitor that speaks every era of video fluently, which is exactly why it plays the bridge in this collection.

At 800 TVL on SMPTE-C phosphors the picture is broadcast-honest. Colors sit precisely where the mastering engineer put them, and 240p sources take on that etched, dimensional quality only a fine-pitch HR Trinitron delivers — the look people chase for years and then refuse to give up.

The practical genius runs deeper. Inputs arrive in pairs with loop-throughs, so it drops into any chain without ceremony, and its one option slot carries a BKM-129X for SCART, VGA and RGB. Even the flyback is shared with the 14L5 and a BVM cousin, the kind of deep parts commonality that keeps a legend alive across decades. Kings age well when the bloodline runs deep.

> One monitor that speaks every era of video fluently — the bridge from 240p to HD.

## Inputs, formats, and what it takes

- **Formats**: 240p, 480i/p, 576i/p, 1035i, 1080i, 720p
- **Sync**: 15–33.75 kHz class multiscan
- **Composite**: 2× with loop-through

title: Sony BVM-20E1U: Specs, BKM Cards & Work Log
description: The grail. One thousand TV lines at twenty inches in 4:3 — a number Sony hit once, on this chassis, and never again.
text:
[Photo: Sony BVM-20E1U broadcast monitor lit in its rack, with an AMS-100 audio monitor speaker on top]

***In the fleet** — BVM broadcast, E/F series — highest-resolution grade*

 Monitor Profile

# Sony BVM-20E1U

The grail. One thousand TV lines at twenty inches in 4:3 — a number Sony hit once, on this chassis, and never again.
 FamilyBVMSize20"Resolution1000 TVLEra1995–2002

Every collector has one machine that justifies the whole pursuit. This is that machine. One thousand TVL, at twenty inches, in 4:3 — a number Sony hit exactly once, on exactly this chassis, and never again. A grail earns the name on a single specification.

Inside is the M49LCB22X, an aperture grille so fine — roughly a quarter of a millimeter — that even the tube in its celebrated successor is coarser. This is the sharpest large-format 4:3 glass ever to leave the company, built in an era when a master control room would clear its budget for the reference seat. Today that reference seat belongs to something better: games.

Because here is the beautiful part — it is a standard-definition instrument by design. 240p and 480i are not formats it tolerates; they are what it is for. Feed it a Saturn or a Neo Geo and the scanline definition is as sharp as the format has ever been rendered, anywhere, by anything. This is the definitive large-format 240p display, and there is no asterisk on that sentence.

It is also a machine you get to build. Four option slots wait behind the fixed RGB block, and the full E/F card family runs to eight — a whole deck of possibilities. Composite is covered, and the S-Video path runs through a BKM-24N that is already on the shelf. Half the joy of a flagship is finishing it.

Sightings are rare enough to count as events. A sound example surfaces perhaps once a season, then vanishes into someone's climate-controlled bay — which is what grail tier actually means: not extravagance, but patience. This one's patience traces to June 2007 build stock, still holding a picture with no living rival.

> Strictly SD forever. That is not the compromise — it is the specification.

## Inputs, formats, and what it takes

- **Formats**: 240p, 480i, 576i only — strictly SD by design
- **Sync**: 15 kHz only
- **Composite**: Via E/F BKM decoder boards — owned BKM-21D covers it
- **Y/C**: Via BKM-24N (owned, on the shelf) or BKM-27T
- **RGB / component**: 1 fixed RGB/component + slots (fixed input block with loop-through)
- **SD-SDI**: Optional (BKM-20D/21D — both owned)
- **HD-SDI**: None
- **Option slots**: 4 + fixed RGB input — full E/F 8-card family
- **Control**: Built-in panel; IC memory card; ISR/RS-485; optional BKM-10R remote
- **Weight**: ~85 lb est. (spec unverified)

## Work log

What has been done to it since it arrived.

- **BKM-21D SDI multi decoder installed** — SDI 4:2:2 and 4fsc in and out, plus analog composite, in one of the four option slots.
- **BKM-24N on the shelf** — The NTSC decoder for composite and Y/C, owned and ready.
- **BKM-20D on the shelf** — The second SDI decoder, owned and ready; the hunt for the E/F-series decoder cards continues on the wanted list (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html).

- **Family**: **Sony BVM** — HR Trinitron CRT (E-grade tube)
- **Era**: **1995–2002** — Native scan — the definitive large-format 240p display; razor scanline definition at 1000 TVL
- **Status**: **Flagship** — The SD reference of the fleet, and the sole E/F-series chassis here.

The open slots are the inputs. Which cards it takes, what each one does, and which ones are still being hunted is on the wanted list (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html#bkm); the bench notes are on Projects (https://www.orlandu.com/projects.html).

title: Sony BVM-A14F5U: Specs, BKM Cards & Work Log
description: The finale. Sony's last CRT generation in fourteen inches — master grade, two of its three card slots filled.
text:
[Photo: Sony BVM-A14F5U broadcast monitor with its full control panel and an AMS-100 speaker above]

***In the fleet** — BVM-A broadcast, final CRT generation*

 Monitor Profile

# Sony BVM-A14F5U

The finale. Sony's last CRT generation in fourteen inches — master grade, two of its three card slots filled.
 FamilyBVM-ASize14"Resolution800 TVLEra2003–2007

Every great saga needs a finale, and the A-series is how Sony's CRT story ends: one final generation, built with everything the company had learned, released into a world already turning to flat panels. The A14F5U is that finale in fourteen inches — the master-grade CRT perfected at the exact moment it became art.

It behaves like something from a later century. Beam landing correction and digital uniformity iron the image flat into the corners in a way no analog-era chassis can approach. A calibration probe hangs on the front of the glass and walks the white point to D65 by measurement rather than by eye. The monitor's entire personality — every setting, every trim — saves to a Memory Stick and travels with you.

It was born to work in packs. Ethernet remote, addressing for a wall of thirty-two units, a control system designed for facilities that ran monitors the way server rooms run racks. In a home bay, all that engineering distills to one thing: total, casual command over a reference-grade picture.

And this one is nearly there. Two of the three option slots are filled: HD-SDI, and an analog board that adds SCART, component and VGA beyond anything the factory ever offered. The third slot, for a BKM-61D and its SD-SDI and S-Video inputs, is still open.

> The master-grade CRT, perfected at the exact moment it became art.

## Inputs, formats, and what it takes

- **Formats**: 240p, 480i/p, 576i/p, 720p, 1080i, 1080/24PsF
- **Sync**: 15–45 kHz
- **Composite**: Via option boards
- **Y/C**: Via BKM-61D (slot open)
- **RGB / component**: Via BKM-68X (clone installed)
- **SD-SDI**: Via BKM-61D (slot open)
- **HD-SDI**: Via BKM-62HS (installed)
- **Option slots**: 3 (68X clone + 62HS installed; one open)
- **Control**: Built-in panel; Ethernet remote; Memory Stick setup save; RS-485 (32 monitors)
- **Weight**: ~48 lb

## Work log

What has been done to it since it arrived.

- **BKM-68X analog input board fitted** — The analog component and RGB board for the A series — a clone, since originals are close to unobtainable — adding SCART, component and VGA the factory never offered.
- **BKM-62HS HD-SDI board fitted** — HD-SDI input in the second slot.
- **Full service by SavonPat, 2025** — Fully converged and aligned; the beam-landing and uniformity systems doing what they were built for.

- **Family**: **Sony BVM** — HR Trinitron CRT
- **Era**: **2003–2007** — Native scan
- **Status**: **In service** — Two of three option slots filled; SD and HD reference with an AMS-100 on top.

title: Sony LMD-9020, 9030, 9050 & 940W: The LMD Wall
description: Mission control. Four LMD models, nine units, one job: keep every signal honest before it reaches the tubes.
text:
[Photo: Three Sony LMD professional LCD monitors side by side, all showing the same cartoon frame]

***In the fleet** — the confidence layer behind the tubes*

 Monitor Profile

# The LMD Wall

Mission control. Four LMD models, nine units, one job: keep every signal honest before it reaches the tubes.
 FamilySony LMDModelsFourUnitsNinePanels8.4" and 9" LCD

Behind the tubes stands mission control. Four LMD models, nine units, one job: keep every signal honest before it touches the glass that matters. Five 9030s form the wall, two 9050s extend it into HD, a 9020 holds the analog corner, and a lone 940W speaks every modern format down to HDMI.

Flip the wall on and the appeal is immediate — identical faces lighting in sequence, one instrument with nine eyes. The 8.4-inch family shares a chassis, a menu system and a single manual, so the whole array behaves like one machine with three signal grades. Run all of it at once and it still draws less power than the flagship CRT does alone.

The 940W is the future-proofing move: ChromaTRU color in 10-bit, one BNC that auto-detects everything from SD through 3G, HDMI for anything made this decade, waveform and audio meters built in, and a tally lamp up top — a broadcast truck condensed into four and a half pounds. In a collection built around glass, this is the crew that keeps the show running.

> Nine screens, one job: keep the signal honest before it reaches a tube.

## Inputs, formats, and what it takes

- **LMD-940W**: 9" wide, 800×480; 3G/HD/SD-SDI on one auto-detecting BNC, HDMI, composite; ChromaTRU color, waveform and audio meters
- **LMD-9020**: 8.4", 640×480; composite, Y/C, component and RGB — the analog corner, no SDI
- **LMD-9030**: 8.4", 640×480; everything the 9020 has plus SD-SDI in and out, and HD over analog component
- **LMD-9050**: 8.4", 1024×768; everything the 9030 has plus HD-SDI

## Work log

What has been done to it since it arrived.

- **LMD-9050 stands fitted** — The two HD-SDI units on their desk stands rather than rack ears.
- **Distribution amp behind the wall** — A CE Labs AV901-HD feeds every unit the same frame at the same instant — the whole path is in The Signal Chain (https://www.orlandu.com/signal-chain.html).

- **Family**: **Sony LMD** — TFT LCD, 8.4-inch chassis family plus the 9-inch 940W.
- **Era**: **2005 onward** — Scaled and deinterlaced — confidence monitors, not the reference glass.
- **Status**: **The wall** — Five LMD-9030s, two LMD-9050s, an LMD-9020 and an LMD-940W.

More photos in the gallery → (https://www.orlandu.com/gallery.html#tag=lmd-wall)

Nearly every home console here reaches a CRT over analog RGB, through a pair of SCART switchers and a stack of BNC breakout cables. The Signal Chain (https://www.orlandu.com/signal-chain.html) shows the whole path.

[Photo: GSCART automatic SCART switch on a clear acrylic mount, eight SCART cables plugged in]

***The GSCART switch** — every SCART lead on this page lands here, and whichever console powers on gets the line to the glass*

[Photo: Lit display shelf of retro consoles at night with two Sony PVM monitors showing Super Mario Bros above]

***The shelf after dark** — Super Mario Bros. on the PVMs, hardware lit like a museum case*

## What was done, and how it reaches the glass

The part every collector asks about: which machines needed a modification to give up RGB, which had it from the factory, and how each one lands on a professional monitor. The path is the same for nearly all of them — an RGB SCART cable into an auto-switcher, a SCART to 4 BNC breakout cable out of it, and a Sony BNC input at the end. Cable makers are left out on purpose; the gear is named.

| Console | Work done | Video out | Into the chain |
|---|---|---|---|
| NES Front Loader · Top Loader | NESRGB board in each | RGB (modded) | RGB SCART → switcher → breakout → PVM / BVM |
| Super Nintendo | Stock | RGB (native) | RGB SCART → switcher → breakout → PVM / BVM |
| Nintendo 64 | RGB upgrade | RGB (modded) | RGB SCART → switcher → breakout → PVM / BVM |
| GameCube | Stock | Component, OEM cable | Component input, no switcher in the path |
| Genesis Model 1 | HDG S-Video and stereo output jacks | RGB (native) · S-Video added | RGB SCART → switcher → breakout → PVM / BVM |
| Genesis CDX | New laser lens | RGB (native) | RGB SCART → switcher → breakout → PVM / BVM |
| Saturn | Stock | RGB (native) | RGB SCART → switcher → breakout → PVM / BVM |
| PC Engine Duo-R | Region mod · RGB mod | RGB (modded) | RGB SCART → switcher → breakout → PVM / BVM |
| PlayStation 2 Slim | MemCard Pro 2 with FMCB/OPL | Component | Switcher → distribution amp → the LMD wall |

This table as open data: JSON (https://www.orlandu.com/data/console-video-out.json) · CSV (https://www.orlandu.com/data/console-video-out.csv) — CC BY 4.0, credit Orlandu’s Arcade.

Handhelds, the unit on the bench, and anything that does not run through the RGB chain are left off. “Switcher” is the GSCARTSW in each room; “breakout” is the SCART to 4 BNC cable. The whole path, box by box, is in The Signal Chain (https://www.orlandu.com/signal-chain.html). Nintendo’s official Player’s Guides have a shelf of their own (https://www.orlandu.com/guide-shelf.html).

title: Nintendo NES Top Loader (NES-101)
description: The NES-101 top loader, Nintendo’s 1993 redesign of the NES, fitted with an NESRGB board so it reaches the Sony monitors in RGB.
text:
[Photo: Nintendo Entertainment System top loader, the NES-101 redesign, with its red power switch]

***On the shelf** — NES-101*

 Console Profile

# NES — Top Loader

Nintendo’s 1993 redesign of the NES. Out of the box it only spoke RF; this one puts out RGB.
 MakerNintendoModelNES-101Year1993VideoRGB (modded)

Nintendo sold the top loader at the very end of the NES’s run: a smaller, cheaper box with the cartridge going straight down, the way the Famicom always had it. It dropped the front loader’s spring-loaded tray and the lockout chip along with it, so the blinking-screen ritual of the original console never happens here.

It also dropped the front loader’s AV jacks. Stock, the top loader speaks RF only, the weakest picture the NES ever had.

The NESRGB board fixes that at the source. It takes the color straight from the console’s picture chip, so this NES joins the rest of the shelf in RGB: an RGB SCART cable into the switcher, a SCART to 4 BNC breakout out of it, and a Sony monitor at the end.

## What it puts out, and how it gets to the glass

- **Stock output**: RF only
- **Modification**: NESRGB board
- **Video out**: RGB over SCART
- **Into the chain**: RGB SCART → switcher → breakout → PVM / BVM
- **Lockout chip**: None — removed by Nintendo in this revision
- **Cartridges**: Top-loading, 72-pin, NTSC

## Work log

What has been done to it.

- **NESRGB board installed** — RGB taken from the picture chip itself, ahead of any RF or composite stage.

- **Family**: **Nintendo NES** — 8-bit, 1985 in North America
- **Revision**: **NES-101** — 1993, the top-loading redesign
- **Status**: **In service** — On the display shelf, wired into the RGB chain.

The console mod table (https://www.orlandu.com/consoles.html#mods) lists every machine’s path to the monitors, and The Signal Chain (https://www.orlandu.com/signal-chain.html) walks it box by box. The NES Front Loader carries an NESRGB board too; it isn’t on the display shelf. Nintendo’s 1996 cartridge holdout. The American N64 never put RGB on its back; this one does.

The Nintendo 64 reached North America in September 1996, the last major home console built around cartridges. Four controller ports on the front made it the multiplayer machine of its generation.

Its video is the catch. The American console sends composite and S-Video out of its multi-out and nothing else; RGB isn’t on the connector at all.

The RGB upgrade puts it there, so the N64 takes the same road to the monitors as the rest of the shelf: an RGB SCART cable into the switcher, a SCART to 4 BNC breakout out of it, and a Sony monitor at the end.

Nintendo folded the Game Boy Advance in half in 2003: a clamshell that protects its own screen, a built-in rechargeable battery, and, for the first time on a Game Boy, a light for the screen. Cobalt was one of the launch colors.

[Photo: Sega Genesis CDX combo unit seen from above, disc lid and player controls visible]

***On the shelf** — MK-4121*

 Console Profile

# Genesis CDX

A Genesis and a Sega CD in one slim 1994 box, running on a replaced laser lens.
 MakerSegaModelMK-4121Year1994VideoRGB (native)

The CDX put a Genesis and a Sega CD in one box barely bigger than a portable CD player, and it doubles as one, with a small display for audio discs. It plays Genesis cartridges on top and Sega CD discs under the lid.

Like every Genesis, it carries RGB on its AV port from the factory, so it needs no mod to reach the monitors: a Genesis 2 style RGB SCART cable into the switcher, a SCART to 4 BNC breakout out of it, and a Sony at the end.

The weak point on any CD system is the laser. This one’s has been replaced, and two more of the same Sanyo pickup sit on the shelf for the next time.

## What it puts out, and how it gets to the glass

- **Video out**: RGB (native)
- **Modification**: None needed
- **Into the chain**: RGB SCART → switcher → breakout → PVM / BVM
- **Media**: Genesis cartridges, Sega CD discs, audio CDs
- **Laser pickup**: Sanyo SF-C93AQ (replaced)
- **Power**: OEM MK-4122 supply

## Work log

What has been done to it.

- **Laser lens replaced** — A new pickup, so discs read cleanly again.
- **Spare pickups on the shelf** — Two more SF-C93AQ lasers, kept for later.

- **Family**: **Sega Genesis + Sega CD** — 16-bit, 1989 and 1992 in North America

# PC Engine Duo-R

NEC’s 1993 HuCard-and-CD machine from Japan, modded for RGB and for the American TurboGrafx library.
 MakerNECRegionJapanYear1993VideoRGB (modded)

The Duo put the PC Engine and its CD-ROM² drive in one white case, and the Duo-R was its 1993 revision. In Japan the PC Engine was a major platform; in America, sold as the TurboGrafx-16, it stayed a cult machine.

Two mods make it the one PC Engine the room needs. A region mod lets it run American TurboGrafx HuCards, which are wired differently from Japanese ones, and an RGB mod brings out a picture the stock console only offers as composite.

A spare laser pickup for the Duo family sits on the shelf for the day the drive needs it.

 Console Profile

# PlayStation 2 Slim

Sony’s 2004 slimline PS2, loading its library from a memory card and feeding the LMD wall over component.
 MakerSonyModelSlimlineYear2004VideoComponent

The slim PlayStation 2 arrived in 2004 at a fraction of the original’s size, with the network adapter built in.

This one runs its games from a MemCard Pro 2. The card sits in the memory card slot, boots Free McBoot, and Open PS2 Loader plays games from its SD card, so the disc drive stays idle. Nothing inside the console is modified.

It is also the one console here that doesn’t take the SCART road. Its component output goes through the switcher to a CE Labs AV901-HD distribution amplifier, which feeds the LMD wall.

- **Into the chain**: Switcher → distribution amp → the LMD wall
- **Distribution amp**: CE Labs AV901-HD
- **Network**: Built-in adapter

How it’s set up.

- **Family**: **PlayStation 2** — 2000 in North America

title: The Signage Wall: Toppers, Cards & Signs
description: Nintendo retail signs, nineteen original PlayChoice-10 toppers and eighteen VS. instruction cards — the print that told an arcade what was in the cabinet.
text:
Paper, Plastic and Fiber Optic

# The Signage Wall

An arcade cabinet is a box that plays one game. Everything that told you *which* game — the topper on the crown, the instruction card on the face, the sign over the counter — was printed, disposable, and thrown out the week it stopped being current. That is why it is rare now. Three walls of it here: the retail signs, nineteen PlayChoice-10 toppers, and eighteen VS. instruction cards.
 Retail Signs Toppers Instruction Cards

## Nintendo retail signage the store stuff

None of this ever ran a game. It hung in a toy store, or over a rental counter, and its whole job was to make a kid stop walking. Three of them survived that job and now light the game room.

In the late 1980s Nintendo stopped leaving its shelf space to the stores. Under a program it called **World of Nintendo**, it shipped retailers a complete *store within a store* — logo signage, banners, hardware and software displays, playable demo stations — so its section looked like Nintendo’s own, whatever chain it sat in. The lighted signs hung above it all. They were store fixtures, not merchandise — made to hang until the next display program replaced them.

***Kay·Bee × World of Nintendo** — the co-branded fiber optic, both panels lit*

 Fiber optic · 1990

### Kay·Bee × World of Nintendo
 LightFiber optic, animated Made1990 Part no.M36C Size6 ft × 18 in

The one sign in the room that names a store. Kay-Bee Toys started in 1922 as the Kaufman brothers’ candy wholesale business in Massachusetts — the name is just their initials, K.B. — and became the toy store in the mall: 1,324 of them by 1999, the second-largest toy chain in the country. This is the co-branded version of Nintendo’s fiber optic sign, six feet of it, with **Kay·Bee** in points of light beside the World of Nintendo oval. It was made for Kay-Bee stores in 1990.

Kay-Bee closed its last stores in early 2009, and its fixtures went with it. Its fiber mechanism still works perfectly: the letters shift color and sparkle through a cycle of about 30 seconds, which is exactly what the loop above shows, start to finish.

***The racetrack** — NESM36F, the oval that gives it the name*

 Fiber optic · NESM36F

### The NES Racetrack
 LightFiber optic, animated Part no.NESM36F SizeAbout 36 × 16 × 8 in Cycle12 seconds

Collectors call the Nintendo oval “the racetrack,” and this sign is nothing but the racetrack: the wordmark in white light, ringed by two red tracks, about 530 points of light in all. Behind the face, a single lamp feeds a bundle of optical fibers, and every point on the face is the end of one fiber. As the sign runs, the letters go from white to red and back, and the pattern repeats exactly every 12 seconds.

Out of the box and on display in the game room, with its fiber mechanism still working perfectly.

[Photo: World of Nintendo Superbrite sign lit head on, yellow World of over the red Nintendo oval]

***The Superbrite** — fluorescent, straight on, no glare*

 Fluorescent · Superbrite series

### World of Nintendo Superbrite
 Light3 × F25T12 fluorescent Part no.M36R SizeAbout 36 × 16 × 6 in Built byThomas A. Schutz Co.

From across a store it reads as neon. There is no neon in it. Three F25T12 fluorescent tubes light the face from behind — that is the *Superbrite* idea, the look of a tube sign from ordinary fluorescents. It was built by the Thomas A. Schutz Co. of Morton Grove, Illinois, whose lighted signs also advertised beer brands.

The World of Nintendo logo is printed on both sides, but only one side lights. It was most likely made to hang in a window: lit toward the street, still readable from inside the store. This is the full logo in Nintendo’s colors, yellow **World of** over the red oval.

## The PlayChoice-10 topper wall nineteen originals

A PlayChoice-10 held ten games at once, so the cabinet needed a way to say what was in it. Nintendo's answer was the topper: a printed sticker, applied to a metal stand that screws to the top of the cabinet, announcing the game — usually with the word *NEW* somewhere on it, because the whole point was to tell a room full of quarters that something had changed. Operators swapped them as the game cards rotated, which is exactly why so few survived: they were consumables, printed to be replaced. The boards they advertised have a wall of their own — all fifty-two PlayChoice-10 game boards (https://www.orlandu.com/playchoice-10.html).

These nineteen are originals, and the copyright lines printed on them run from Gauntlet's 1985 to the Turtles' 1990. They were printed for PlayChoice-10 cabinets; the canopy of the Red Tent (https://www.orlandu.com/red-tent.html) is simply where they get displayed. More of them are still on the hunt list (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html).

## The VS. instruction card wall eighteen cards

The Nintendo VS. System was a cabinet with a swappable board. Change the PCB and the machine became a different game — which left the operator holding a cabinet that no longer said what it was. The instruction card was the fix: a square of printed paper, fixed to the face beside the controls, carrying the title, the button layout and the rules in about two hundred words. Every card here was printed for one specific machine: the VS. DualSystem cocktail — the Red Tent (https://www.orlandu.com/red-tent.html) in the game room.

Change the board, swap the card. It is paper, so it could go back in the drawer until that board went in again — most carry a small adhesive strip on the back, a few have no adhesive at all, and one, Top Gun, is a full sticker. These eighteen are operator stock that never went on a cabinet. Eleven are Nintendo’s own titles; six carry a licensee’s name printed right on the card, because the VS. System was a platform Nintendo rented out; the last is the PlayChoice channel-select card. Three more are still on the hunt list (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html).

A PlayChoice-10 cabinet held ten games at once, and each game arrived as its own bare circuit board. The whole library, board by board.
 The Wall Conversions What a Board Is Elsewhere

The ROMs sit in sockets, a Nintendo part number runs silkscreened down the middle, and a printed title label goes on the front. No shell, no artwork, nothing to protect it — these were never meant to be seen by anyone but the operator who swapped them. Click any board to open it full size.

## Conversions ten boards Nintendo never made

Some of these are games that never had a PlayChoice release at all, moved onto real PlayChoice hardware. Others are the same title running a different build of the game. What nearly all of them share is a save battery — the one thing a coin-op board has no reason to carry, and the one thing each of these games cannot do without.

[Photo: Baseball Stars PlayChoice-10 conversion board with a save battery fitted]

### Baseball Stars battery save

Baseball Stars had a PlayChoice release of its own, but with its heart cut out: exhibition games, and nothing else. Everything the game is remembered for lived behind a save battery on the NES cartridge — the first sports game on the system to carry one — where you built your own team, named every player on it, and ran a league season of up to 125 games while the statistics piled up. This board puts the battery back, so that version is the one that comes up at a cabinet.

[Photo: Dragon Warrior on a converted PlayChoice-10 board with save battery]

### Dragon Warrior

No PlayChoice board ever carried Dragon Warrior, and it is not hard to see why: a cabinet that charges by the minute is the last place anyone would put a sixty-hour role-playing game. This is a conversion with a save battery fitted, which is the only thing that makes the idea work at all — the adventure survives the cabinet being switched off.

[Photo: Final Fantasy on a converted PlayChoice-10 board]

### Final Fantasy

Square’s role-playing game, out in Japan at the end of 1987 and in America in 1990. You name four characters, choose what each of them is, and the decisions made in the first ten minutes are still with you thirty hours later when the class change turns them into something else. All of that lives in one save file, which is the whole reason no arcade board ever carried the game and the reason this one has a battery on it.

[Photo: Hello Kitty World on a converted PlayChoice-10 board]

### Hello Kitty World

A Famicom exclusive from 1992, published by Character Soft and never sold outside Japan. Under the Sanrio artwork it is Balloon Kid — the Game Boy sequel to Balloon Fight — redrawn. Getting it onto a PlayChoice board meant burning ROMs for hardware the game had never met; a friend of the arcade did that work.

[Photo: The Legend of Zelda on a custom PlayChoice-10 board with built-in save]

### The Legend of Zelda

Zelda was never part of the PlayChoice library, which is a shame — a cabinet with a second screen showing instructions above the game is exactly what a 1986 dungeon crawl wanted. This is a fully custom board with the save hardware designed in rather than bodged on.

[Photo: Metroid on a custom PlayChoice-10 board running the save and map hack]

### Metroid map + save

Metroid was a PlayChoice title, so this one is not about a missing game — it is about which build of it you play. The board runs the community hack that throws out the password screen for three save files and adds a scrolling map to the pause menu, with the battery on board to hold them. It is the version of Metroid everyone wishes had shipped.

[Photo: Shadowgate on a converted PlayChoice-10 board with save battery]

### Shadowgate

Another with no PlayChoice release of its own. A point-and-click adventure where death is one wrong verb away, running on a machine that charges by the minute — the save battery is doing a great deal of work here.

[Photo: Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels on a converted PlayChoice-10 board]

### Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels

The Japanese Super Mario Bros. 2, out on the Famicom Disk System in 1986 and turned down for America as unfairly hard. Nintendo shipped a reworked Doki Doki Panic under that name instead, and *that* is the Super Mario Bros. 2 up on the wall. This board carries the original: poison mushrooms, wind, and a warp pipe that sends you backwards.

[Photo: VS. Duck Hunt on a custom PlayChoice-10 board carrying both the arcade and console versions]

### VS. Duck Hunt

The arcade Duck Hunt is not the console one. The VS. build runs its rounds in sequence and finishes on a bonus stage the home version never had — the same kind of gap that separates VS. Super Mario Bros. from the game everyone grew up on. This custom board carries both versions.

[Photo: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link on a converted PlayChoice-10 board with save battery]

### Zelda II: The Adventure of Link

No PlayChoice release either, so: a conversion, battery fitted. Necessary for a game that expects to take your three lives and see you again tomorrow.

## What a board is and what it is not

The PlayChoice-10 arrived in 1986 and solved an operator’s problem rather than a player’s. A cabinet plays one game; a cabinet that plays ten earns ten times as many chances at the same quarter. Inside is a motherboard with ten slots, and each game is one of these boards plugged into it. Coins buy *time*, not lives, and the clock runs across the whole menu — pick a game, die in thirty seconds, pick another and keep going until the timer stops.

The hardware underneath is a Nintendo Entertainment System, which is why the library reads like a shelf of NES boxes. It is not an NES, though, and a board like this will not run in one: the ROMs sit behind the PlayChoice’s own security and menu hardware, and the cabinet expects a second screen full of instructions above the game.

Look along the chips on any board here and you will find the same two letters repeated on every one — Nintendo’s internal code for the title, stamped on each ROM so an operator or a repair tech could tell at a glance that all the pieces belonged together. The labels are the quickest way to read a board when the title sticker has come off:

- **BF** Balloon Fight
- **CT** Contra
- **DH** Duck Hunt
- **DW** Double Dribble
- **EB** Excitebike
- **GL** Gauntlet
- **MA** Mario Bros.
- **MT** Metroid
- **NG** Ninja Gaiden
- **RA** Rush’n Attack
- **SM** Super Mario Bros.
- **YW** Captain Skyhawk

The part number tells you the rest. Every board is stamped **PCH1** and then a revision — **PCH1-01-ROM** through **PCH1-04-ROM**, with a letter suffix — and the later the game, the busier the board: the earliest titles here are three fat EPROMs and a handful of logic chips, while the last ones carry a surface-mount Nintendo mapper and far less socketed anything. Two titles, Captain Skyhawk and Solar Jetman, use a board type of their own, which is the usual reason a set build stalls one or two short of the end.

## Elsewhere the rest of the PlayChoice-10

### The topper wall (https://www.orlandu.com/signage.html#toppers)
 Signage

The printed sticker that sat on the crown of the cabinet and announced which game had just gone in. Nineteen originals hang on the signage wall — the paper half of this hobby, and much harder to find than the boards.

### The cabinets (https://www.orlandu.com/games.html#memoriam)
 Coin-Op Games

The uprights and counter-tops that these boards were built for passed through here on their way to somewhere else. They are in the memoriam on the coin-op page.

### The hunt list (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html)
 Wanted

The boards are finished; the toppers are not. Every PlayChoice-10 topper still being looked for is on the wanted list, with a way to get in touch if one is sitting in your garage.

text:
Maps, Codes and Cover Art

# The Strategy Guide Shelf

A strategy guide was a book you bought because the game would not tell you where to go. Nintendo printed its own through Nintendo Power — hand-drawn maps, enemy tables and the routes the designers expected you to miss — and gave most of them commissioned cover art that appeared nowhere else. That is the part worth hanging on a wall: a shelf of these reads less like a stack of manuals than like a run of illustration. Twenty-one here, photographed one cover at a time.

Here for the *monitor* buying guide instead? What to Check Before You Buy a PVM-20L5 (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-20l5-buying-guide.html) is over in Stories.

## The shelf twenty-one guides

text:
The gallery is lit, in-room photography of the machines and monitors. Captions:

- **Kay·Bee × World of Nintendo**: The co-branded fiber optic with both panels lit — mall-era retail glow, intact. The signage wall →
- **PVM-2950Q**: The 29-inch presence in the game room, lit at night with Super Mario World on the tube. The fleet →
- **The Red Tent, reborn**: Fresh paint, serviced monitors, polished chrome — forty years younger. The restoration story →
- **VS. Super Mario Bros.**: The UniSystem doing what it does best, pixel-art invaders keeping watch overhead. The full profile →
- **The shelf of accomplices**: Gundam, Rick and Morty, and a full Thundercats bench keeping watch over the library
- **Down the garage arcade**: The long view — deck collection overhead, the cabinet row, pinball in the back, and pro monitors wherever they fit. Coin-Op Games →
- **Ghostbusters Premium**: Zombie Yeti artwork lit like a nightclub, magna-slings waiting. The full profile →

- **The garage arcade after dark**: The whole room lit: the cabinet row down one wall, the pinball row down the other. Coin-Op Games →

- **Who's the master?**: The fiber optic Kay·Bee / World of Nintendo sign lit up over the game room wall — Sho'nuff approves, Joy-Con and Wiimote racks standing by, the Red Tent below. The signage wall →

- **The console shelf by day**: Paper Mario on the smaller PVM, Super Mario World on the 29-inch, the shelf lit underneath. The consoles →
