## Appendix E The AMS-3 — Predecessor Candidate

*Source discipline:* this appendix documents four AMS-3 units at two evidence tiers. Two Japan-domestic units, serials 10685 and 11558, read from the EXT-01 photo packs of July 2026 — cited [contributor photo, EXT-01] — in the same Australian custody as the §4.5.1 AMS-100. Two export units, serials 20087 and 20144, acquired by the author in 2026 and read from his own photographs and handling — cited [author] or [author photo] (plates C-35–C-39). No Sony documentation for the AMS-3 is in the project's possession, and no period paperwork accompanied any of the four units. The author's units are **not registry members**: the registry is an AMS-100 record and stands at n = 7 (§4.1); no AMS-3 transaction enters the Section 7 ledger. The lineage claim this appendix examines therefore ends the appendix as unverified as it began — what changes, and it changed twice, is what the AMS-3 is known to have been as a product.

### E.1 The claim, and what this appendix can and cannot do

Sony marketing copy links the AMS-100 to an earlier AMS-3 as its predecessor. The monograph carries that lineage at low confidence (§1.4) because the claim has never been sourced to period Sony engineering or product literature — only to promotional text. Physical units cannot fix that: four AMS-3s on two continents confirm that the product existed, what it was, and how it compares to the AMS-100; they cannot confirm that Sony positioned one as the other's successor. The instrument that would settle the lineage is a period cross-reference — an AMS-3 document naming the AMS-100, or the reverse — and none of the four units carried one. §1.4's confidence flag is unchanged by this appendix, deliberately, and the author's acquisition of two units does not move it: **hardware is not provenance.**

What the appendix does instead: documents the AMS-3 as hardware, and lays the two designs side by side so that the comparative case — continuity of design vocabulary across a generational redesign — is on the record with its evidence, tagged as observation rather than lineage proof.

### E.2 The documented units — two market variants

The four units divide cleanly into two groups, and the division is the appendix's principal finding. It was not visible when only the contributor pair was documented.

| | Unit a | Unit b | Unit c | Unit d |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Serial | 10685 | 11558 | 20087 | 20144 |
| Model-plate part | 2-356-601-01 | identical | 2-356-602-02 | identical |
| Power rating | AC 100 V, 50/60 Hz, 150 W | identical | AC 100/120/220/240 V, 50/60 Hz, 150 W | identical |
| Corporate text | SONY / ソニー株式会社 / Made in Japan | identical | SONY / Sony Corporation / Made in Japan — no Japanese corporate line | identical |
| Date code | none | none | none | none |
| Caution label | 3-703-043-21 (EN/FR bilingual) | identical | 3-703-043-21 (EN/FR bilingual) | identical |
| Rack ears | fitted | absent | fitted | fitted |
| Asset marking | none observed | none observed | institutional barcode tag (E.2.1) | institutional barcode tag (E.2.1) |
| Weight | not measured | not measured | 35 lb (≈ 15.9 kg) | 35 lb (≈ 15.9 kg) |
| Source | [contributor photo, EXT-01] | [contributor photo, EXT-01] | [author photo; weight author-measured] | [author photo; weight author-measured] |

**The variant finding.** Four attributes move together across the two groups: model-plate part number, supply rating, corporate text, and serial band. That is four independent axes agreeing, which is a good deal more than a single differing figure would be, and the reading of record is that **the AMS-3 shipped in at least two market variants** — a Japan-domestic 100 V version and a multi-voltage export version [confidence: moderate-to-high for the two-variant conclusion; the sample is two units per side, and both export units come from a single facility, so nothing here bounds how many variants existed or in what proportion].

**Serial bands.** The domestic pair reads 10685 / 11558 and the export pair 20087 / 20144 — two distinct 1xxxx and 2xxxx bands, correlating with the variant split at n = 2 each. All four sit above 10001, the floor the Installation Manual declares for the AMS-100 family [IM]. Whether the 2xxxx band is a separate export block, a later production period, or coincidence *is not determinable from four units*, and no volume, dating, or rate inference is drawn from any of these numbers [observation only; no confidence assigned].

**The date-free plates extend the family marking-practice finding** (§4.4) backward a product generation and now across both variants: whatever Sony's external-marking policy was for this monitoring line, every AMS-3 plate in the record follows it. The production era of these units is unbracketed by their own surfaces.

#### E.2.1 Institutional asset marking on the export pair

Both export units carry a white adhesive barcode label on the rear panel, beside the model plate, reading PROPERTY OF THE CHRISTIAN SCIENCE PUBLISHING SOCIETY with a barcode and the human-readable strings TVBE-51326 (20087) and TVBE-51320 (20144) [author photo — plates C-36, C-39].

The labels are transcribed here and nothing is inferred from them. No claim is made about the organization, its facilities, its broadcast activities, when it held the units, or how they left its custody; the project has sought no documentation on any of these points and the research program is closed (Appendix F). What the labels establish, and all they establish, is that both export units passed through one institution's asset-tracking system, and that their tag numbers are six apart — the same evidentiary shape as the consecutive UAE seal serials of §4.4, and the second instance in this project of two units of one purchase carrying near-adjacent third-party identifiers. The tags are the only provenance either export unit carries.

### E.3 Physical description

**Format.** 2RU rack unit — twice the AMS-100's height — with two internal speakers behind metal grilles flanking a central meter block, and a measured mass of 35 lb (≈ 15.9 kg) on the export units [author, measured]. This is the project's only weight figure for any product of the family: the corresponding AMS-100 measurement is declined by standing ruling (A.1), and the two figures should not be read against one another as a like-for-like comparison. The ソニー株式会社 plate text and 100 V-only rating mark the contributor units as Japan-domestic; the author's units are marked for four supply voltages (E.2). On both variants the 150 W rating is matched by a prominent finned heatsink running the chassis side [contributor photo, EXT-01]: a substantially larger amplifier stage than the successor's (the AMS-100 draws 25 W [IM]), and the readiest explanation of the mass.

**Front panel.** POWER rocker with separate indicator window; two illuminated analog VU meters (−20 to +3 scale with a percentage-modulation scale beneath, red segment above 0) labeled INPUT LEVEL L/R; two rotary SP LEVEL pots (0–10 scale), one per channel; the legend AUDIO MONITOR SPEAKER AMS-3 across the meter block. **No input selection of any kind** — what the rear receives is what the speakers monitor. Panel finish on the export units is light gray [author photo, plate C-37].

**Rear panel.** Fixed, analog-only I/O, identical in complement across both variants:

| Facility | Detail |
|---|---|
| Inputs, per channel | XLR-32F (male) + XLR-31F (female) pair, ITT Cannon — true loop-through |
| Input impedance, per channel | slide switch: 600 Ω / 10 kΩ / HIGH |
| Input level, per channel | slide switch: 8 dB / 4 dB / 0 dB |
| Speaker routing | SPEAKER SELECT slide: INT. / EXT. |
| External speakers | EXT SPEAKER R/L XLR pair, 8 Ω |
| Other | ground post; IEC AC inlet; one covered rotary component (see below) |

Rear-panel readings for the domestic pair [contributor photo, EXT-01]; connector types and switch legends corroborated at author tier on the export pair [author photo, plate C-38]. Switch functions are read from panel legends, not verified electrically.

**One unresolved fitting.** A large rotary component under a clear protective cover sits at the right of the rear panel on all four units. It was recorded as a fuse holder when only the domestic pair was documented. On a chassis marked for four supply voltages, a covered *voltage selector* is at least as likely, and the protective cover is more characteristic of a selector than of a fuse; the legend beneath the cover is not readable in any photograph in hand. The identification is left open [candidate reading, flagged not ruled — no examination was made, and none is scheduled (Appendix F)]. If it is a selector, its presence on the domestic 100 V-only units would itself be worth knowing, and nothing in the record settles that either.

### E.4 The comparative reading — design vocabulary across a generation

Laid against the AMS-100 (Sections 2–3), the AMS-3 reads as the same monitoring concept executed a hardware generation earlier. The continuities and the breaks are both instructive; all of the following is comparative observation from documented hardware on each side, *not lineage evidence*:

**What carried forward.** The per-channel input-conditioning grammar is recognizably continuous: switched impedance including a 600 Ω termination position, switched input level, XLR loop-through per channel. The AMS-100's BKAM-101 analog board speaks a terser dialect of the same language — 600 Ω termination on/off, +4/0 dB level [IM][MM] — where the AMS-3 offers three positions on each axis (600 Ω / 10 kΩ / HIGH; 8/4/0 dB). The loop-through convention survives the generation intact, reappearing on the 101's connector pairs [MM] and even on the 103's SDI BNC pair.

**What the redesign changed.** Three moves, each in the same direction — from a self-contained analog monitor toward a compact, system-integrated one:

1. **Fixed I/O → modular slots.** The AMS-3's hardwired analog inputs became the AMS-100's two-slot option architecture (Section 3) — the defining change, and the one that makes the successor's configuration a documentable variable at all.
2. **Analog VU → LED bar metering**, with the AMS-100 adding front-panel input selection and calibration modes the AMS-3 has no equivalent for.
3. **On-board external-speaker facility dropped.** The AMS-3 drives external 8 Ω speakers directly, with front-panel INT/EXT routing; the AMS-100 has no frame-level equivalent — amplified line-out moved to the REMOTE connector's monitor-output plane [IM], trading the facility for the 1RU height and the smaller amplifier.

**A fourth move, withdrawn.** Earlier revisions of this appendix listed a fourth: Japan-domestic 100 V → universal 100–240 V supply, read as evidence that the successor was built for worldwide deployment and the predecessor candidate was not. **That reading is withdrawn.** It rested on the two domestic units then in the record, and the appendix flagged its own exposure at the time — whether export-market AMS-3 variants existed was stated as unknown. The author's units answer it: they exist, and the AMS-3 was sold into multiple mains markets.

What survives is narrower, and is a statement about supply architecture rather than market ambition: **tap-selected multi-voltage (100/120/220/240 V) → continuous auto-ranging universal supply (100–240 V)** [E.2 vs. IM]. The predecessor candidate reached export markets by offering four discrete voltage settings, presumably selected at installation; the successor reached them with one supply that requires no setting at all. That is a real generational change in how a product is made deployable, and it is a smaller claim than the one it replaces. *The withdrawal is recorded rather than quietly corrected* because the original reading was published, and because it is a clean instance of what this monograph's evidence tiers exist to catch: a confident generalization drawn from n = 2 of one variant, falsified by the next two units to enter the record.

**Weight of the comparison.** The continuity of input-conditioning vocabulary is real and specific — 600 Ω switched termination on a rack confidence monitor is not so generic a feature that its recurrence means nothing. But convergent design within one manufacturer's pro-audio group explains it just as well as direct succession. The comparison makes the lineage plausible; it cannot make it sourced. [author reading of the comparative evidence; moderate for the continuity observation itself, no upgrade to the lineage claim]

### E.5 The lineage question — state and paths

**State: unverified, low confidence, unchanged** (§1.4). Two documentary paths have now returned nothing: period paperwork with the contributor units, and period paperwork with the author's own two — neither group arrived with a manual, a carton, or a document of any kind. *Four units, no paper.* The paths that could in principle move the question are recorded for completeness and are not pursued by this project (Appendix F): a listing carrying AMS-3 manuals, brochures, or boxes in any market [no claim is made about how often such listings appear]; the AMS-100 Operation Manual, not located (§2.8); period Sony broadcast catalogs of the mid-1990s.

That four physically documented units move the lineage claim not at all is the point worth stating plainly. Each new unit sharpens the description of the product and can falsify a comparative reading — as the export pair has just done to E.4's fourth move — while leaving the succession question exactly where marketing copy left it. **The formulation of record stands: the AMS-3 is a documented product and a credible predecessor candidate; the succession itself remains marketing copy.**
 **Sources** EXT-01 photo packs, July 2026 (22 images; intake record in the project file) [contributor photo, EXT-01] — plates C-19–C-21; the author's photographs and handling of AMS-3 units 20087 and 20144, 2026 [author; author photo] — plates C-35–C-39, weight author-measured; Sony Installation Manual [IM] and Maintenance Manual [MM] for all AMS-100-side comparanda. Contributor credit: Appendix D. Bounds for this appendix are stated in Appendix F.

## Appendix F Bounds of the Record

This appendix states where the monograph's record stops. The research program behind it closed in August 2026 by author ruling: no further acquisition, inquiry, recovery, measurement, or observation is scheduled, and nothing below is an open task. Each line names a question the record leaves unanswered, the publication home of the finding it bounds, and the ruling that closes it, so that no reader, contributor, or later editor mistakes a gap for an oversight or reopens a question that was closed on purpose. Frames are identified by serial throughout; the drafting record numbers (R-1 … R-7) map to frame serials at Appendix D, D.3, and nowhere else. This appendix records; it does not decide, rank, or resolve.

### Documentation

- **Operation Manual — not located; search closed.** The third Sony document of the set (§2.8) was confirmed absent from the online manual aggregators at the July 2026 literature sweep, and the physical search is closed. Every figure and statement that only it could have verified stands permanently at its current tier: the dealer-only frame specifications (speakers, headphone output, monitor-output maximum and impedance — §2.4, A.1–A.2); the dealer-only board figures (BKAM-101 maximum level and bridging impedance, BKAM-102 BNC impedance — §3.2, §3.3, A.3–A.4); frame weight and depth (A.1 — measurement declined by ruling); the operator-facing wording of the BKAM-103 channel-select procedure (§3.4) and the behavior of the GP/CH buttons with a BKAM-102 selected (§5.6 — not investigated by experiment); the per-line REM/STS-to-slot mapping and the extent of the level/pulse type beyond pins 14/15 (Appendix B); the AMS-3 lineage (E.5). The D.1 entry is closed as not located.
- **Literature claim is dated.** The statement that no editorial or community literature on the AMS-100 exists (§1.1, §7.1) is a finding of the July 2026 sweep; no periodic re-sweep is scheduled, and the claim publishes as dated, not as standing.
- **Period Sony literature.** The BVM/PVM pairing claim (§1.3) rests on marketing copy, and the AMS-3 lineage (§1.4, Appendix E) stays at low confidence by design; neither a period catalog nor a price list was sought beyond the July 2026 sweep. No dealer inquiry is made for the Operation Manual, loose-board restock, or AMS-3 paperwork.

### Hardware

- **The AMS-3 export pair — documented, not investigated.** Units 20087 and 20144 are described in Appendix E from the author's photographs and handling. Three things about them are recorded and not pursued: the identification of the covered rotary component on the rear panel, left open between a fuse holder and a voltage selector (§E.3) — no examination is scheduled; the institutional asset tags on both units, transcribed and nothing more (§E.2.1) — no enquiry is made of the named organization; and the significance of the 2xxxx serial band, on which four units support no inference (§E.2). AMS-3 20087 has been sold. Neither unit is a registry member and neither generates a Section 7 ledger row.
- **A published reading withdrawn.** Appendix E's former fourth redesign move — Japan-domestic supply giving way to a universal one across the generation — was falsified by the export pair and is withdrawn in place rather than deleted (§E.4). It is recorded here as the record's clearest instance of a generalization drawn from one variant at n = 2 failing against new hardware; the surviving claim is narrower and is about supply architecture only.
- **Registry board-side recheck: declined.** The five-digit serial status of the BKAM-103 labels 0105241 / 0128521 and of 12793's BKAM-102 is permanently unknown. No board is pulled from a working installation for identification, dating, QFP confirmation, or serial reading alone; the BKAM-103 large QFPs (CXB1342R / CXD8280AQ) stay at Maintenance-Manual tier, and the serials of the four Japan-recycler BKAM-101s arriving later are unread (§4.2, §4.4, §6.4).
- **BKAM-102 s/n 10083 — never read, now installed.** Its serial is assigned by elimination against carton S01-0010083 and was never read from the PCB. The board was installed into either frame 12886 or frame 13048 without being read, and 13048 has since been sold, so the carton-to-board mapping closes permanently at two of three (§4.2). Which of the two frames received it, and which received 12793's as-surfaced BKAM-102, is unstated and stays so.
- **Placements and states not recorded.** The individual routing of the four unread BKAM-101s among 10010, 11341, 12793, and 12886, and 11341's slot letters — the census fixes the totals and the origins, not which board sits where (§4.2); the serials of the boards in 12886 and 13048, never read at any point; the cabling of every BKAM-101-fed monitor point, the disposition of the converters, and the splitter state at 12793 at its conversion to analog (§5.2, §5.3); the S101 position of the one installed BKAM-102 (§5.6); the installation role of frame 12886 (§5.3); the 600 Ω as-found switch positions of every BKAM-101 handled (§3.2); the STS level/pulse configuration of every frame (§6.2); the CRT-top placement specifics (§5.5). All are undocumented and stay so.
- **Seal C094182 on frame 10010.** In place as last checked at the author's rebuild; not re-verified since (§4.3, §4.4). Chassis sweeps were not run on 11878, 12886, or 13048 (§4.4).
- **Date-code candidates: not adopted.** Two 2000-family board marks (a five-character mark on a BKAM-101, a six-digit mark on a BKAM-103) stay in the project record; no code-format ruling or board sweep is made. The production window publishes as “at least into 1999” and the end of production as unknown (§1.5, §6.4). Sony external marking for this family is confirmed date-free (seven registry plates, three cartons, the contributor's plate, and all four AMS-3 plates across both market variants).
- **§6.4 discrepancies stand as recorded.** The BKAM-102 CPLD/firmware readings (EPM7064S V1.10 on the contributor's s/n 10016; EPM7032S V1.20 on the author's s/n 10099) and the BKAM-103 per-CPLD firmware readings (V1.00/V1.00 on s/n 10130; V1.10/V1.00 on s/n 10631) are flagged, not reconciled, and no re-verification is made; neither value is tabulated as a family specification (A.4, A.5).
- **HD-SDI option board BKAM-10▮** (§3.1). Attested by one social-media photograph; part number unread; untabulated in Appendix A and outside the Maintenance Manual's coverage statements. EXT-03 is anonymous, uncontacted by ruling, photo-tier only, and closed at opening; its screenshots are not plates.

### Images

- **No image is reproduced.** Every plate in Appendix C publishes as a caption. The twenty author photographs (C-1–C-9, C-24–C-34) are withdrawn from publication and held in the project record; every reading that rested on them stands at [author] tier on that record. The nine EXT-01 images in the project file and the two archived seller-listing files are held, not embedded.
- **C-11 / C-13 / C-18.** Never supplied by the contributor; recovery closed. The BKAM-103 firmware divergence that C-13 would have re-checked stands as a flagged discrepancy (above).
- **C-23 custody.** The second seller-listing archive filename's hash differs from the project's capture record, which lists a “front” as the second file; five distinct files are held against six listing images. Both discrepancies are recorded and stand unreconciled (Appendix C, D.3).

### Market and transactions

- **Author transactions: withheld, not unknown.** No author figure, band, approximation, direction, or ratio publishes; no author transaction date publishes beyond the year; sale particulars beyond event and configuration do not publish; the author's sources publish as exactly three channel classes — a UAE electronics recycler, a Japan electronics recycler, and a US electronics recycler (the sealed BKAM-102 lot) — with no finer characterization; counterparties, dealers, and venues of the author's own transactions are unnamed (§1.1, sole statement). Whether any registry frame is offered for sale at any time is not published; registry status is *held* or *sold* only (§4.1). The author's private record identifiers are not published for any frame (D.3).
- **Third-party prices as observed.** The $999.99 US-visible frame ask (§7.2, §7.3) and a Tokyo dealer's ¥13,200 sold-out loose BKAM-101 listing are July 2026 observations; neither is re-observed, no currency conversion or rounding of either is published, and the ≈2017 US hi-fi reseller sale stays an existence datum with no price (no seller inquiry is made).
- **No rate claims, ever.** Nothing in the record supports a statement of how often AMS-100s or BKAM boards surface in any channel; every population statement is a dated, point-in-time observation (§1.7, §7.1, §7.8). The daily-search observation log is retired and is never cited. No seal-recurrence, loose-board-supply, or per-board BKAM-101 market watch is maintained.
- **EXT-01: no follow-up, no ledger row.** EXT-01's contribution is closed at the credit line of record (Appendix D); provenance beyond custody geography is skipped permanently.

### Labels and record artifacts

- **Compliance and aftermarket labels: out of publication.** The top-cover compliance label present on all seven frames was removed by the author; its partial reading from a listing photograph is the permanent basis and is not published.
- **Name-implied is not data.** REM-A / STS-A → SLOT A and REM-B / STS-B → SLOT B is a naming inference (Appendix B); the select-code and pin tables are verbatim transcriptions and carry no interpretation.
- **Records are outside this monograph.** Amendment of the author's private records for the first three frames, identifiers for the four later frames, the sale record, and the region-field reconciliation are matters of the author's private record and have no publication consequence.
 **Sources** The author's rulings of July–August 2026 closing the research program; the open-item lines formerly carried by Sections 1–7 and Appendices A–E, as consolidated and closed; Sony Installation Manual [IM] and Maintenance Manual [MM] for the manual-coverage statements cited; Appendix D for every record referenced.

title: Sony AMS-3 vs. AMS-100: Ancestor and Descendant
description: Sony's AMS-3 and AMS-100 do the same job thirty years apart — a transformer and a wall of heatsink versus SDI and plug-in cards, stacked one on the other.
text:
Did You Know?

# Ancestor and Descendant

Two Sony audio monitors, built to do the same job in the same kind of room, roughly thirty years apart. Stack one on the other and the entire history of broadcast engineering is sitting on your bench.

Every rack of video monitors needs a way to hear what it is looking at. In a studio or a machine room that job goes to an audio monitor speaker — a self-powered box that takes the audio riding alongside the picture and lets an engineer hear whether it is there, whether it is clipping, and which channel is which. Sony made them for decades. Two of them live here, and they could hardly be less alike.

The **AMS-100** is the modern one, and the one that actually works in the rack in the garage. It is slim, light, and unmistakably digital: SDI in, digital audio in, plug-in option cards, a remote port on the back, bar-graph level meters and a keypad on the front. It is designed to disappear into a rack and be driven by something else.

The **AMS-3** is its ancestor, and it disappears into nothing. It weighs 35 lbs — the same as a 14-inch PVM — because it does its work the old way: a real transformer, a real amplifier, and a bank of heatsink fins deep enough to make the whole chassis twice as tall as the newer unit. Its front panel has two analog VU meters with needles that swing, an input level knob and a speaker level knob, and nothing else. Its back panel wants balanced XLR, with an impedance switch and a level switch per channel, plus outputs for external speakers. And it is *loud* — comfortably loud enough to be heard over a room full of running CRTs, which is exactly the room it was built for.

[Photo: Sony AMS-100 stacked on top of a Sony AMS-3, front panels facing out, showing the AMS-3 is roughly twice as tall]

***Front to front** — AMS-100 on top, AMS-3 below. Bar-graph meters and a keypad above; analog VU needles and two big level knobs beneath*

[Photo: Profile view of the two units stacked, showing the AMS-3's deep heatsink fins against the AMS-100's shallow flat chassis]

***The part that explains the weight** — in profile, the AMS-100 is a flat plate. The AMS-3 is a wall of fins*

The back panels tell the story even more plainly than the profile does. One unit is waiting for a digital stream; the other is waiting for a pair of balanced cables and a decision about impedance. Same shelf, same purpose, two completely different centuries of thinking about how sound gets from one box to another.

[Photo: Rear panels of both units: the AMS-100 with SDI and digital audio inputs and option card slots, the AMS-3 with six XLR connectors and external speaker outputs]

***Back to back** — the AMS-100 wants SDI and digital audio. The AMS-3 wants balanced XLR, with impedance and level switches per channel and outputs for external speakers*

## A previous life

There is one more thing on the back of the AMS-3, and it is the best part. A printed asset tag, still stuck to the chassis, reading **PROPERTY OF THE CHRISTIAN SCIENCE PUBLISHING SOCIETY** — barcoded, numbered, and signed out like a stapler. Before this thing turned up untested in a box in Orange County, it was inventory in somebody's broadcast plant, bolted into a rack, listening to a feed that mattered to somebody's deadline.

That is the whole appeal of professional gear, really. A consumer speaker from 1985 would be landfill by now. This one was built to be racked, powered, ignored, and depreciated for decades — and after all of that, the worst thing wrong with it was a scratchy volume pot. That took a can of fader cleaner and an afternoon. It is off the bench now (https://www.orlandu.com/projects.html).

***After the cleaning** — the SP LEVEL pots quiet again, both VU needles moving, the AMS-3 riding on top of the BVM-20E1U for the test*

The deep technical write-up on the AMS-100 — history, internals, and module configurations — is its own piece (https://www.orlandu.com/ams-100-monograph.html). This one is just about what happens when you put the two of them on top of each other.

## Quick answers

### What is the Sony AMS-3?

Sony's analog audio monitor speaker from the era before the AMS-100 — a self-powered box with a real transformer, a real amplifier, and a bank of heatsink fins that makes the chassis twice as tall as its successor. Two analog VU meters with needles that swing, an input level knob, a speaker level knob, and nothing else on the front. It weighs 35 lb, the same as a 14-inch PVM, and it is loud enough to be heard over a room full of running CRTs.

### What inputs does the AMS-3 take?

Balanced XLR, with an impedance switch and a level switch per channel, plus outputs for external speakers. No digital input of any kind — it is waiting for a pair of balanced cables and a decision about impedance.

### How is the AMS-100 different from the AMS-3?

The AMS-100 is slim, light and digital: SDI in, digital audio in, plug-in option cards, a remote port on the back, bar-graph meters and a keypad on the front, built to disappear into a rack. The AMS-3 does the same job — letting an engineer hear the audio riding alongside the picture — thirty years earlier, in analog. The AMS-100 monograph → (https://www.orlandu.com/ams-100-monograph.html)

## PVM-2950Q
 29" production

[Photo: PVM-2950Q]

*PVM-2950Q*

Every collection has a centerpiece, and this one announces itself before it is ever switched on. The PVM-2950Q is twenty-nine inches of Super Trinitron in a hundred-and-fifteen-pound cube — the biggest tube Sony ever committed to a production monitor, and the closest thing the format has to a monument.

Turn it on and the monument becomes a window. This is arcade-era spectacle at living-room scale: the same glass family the era's games were mastered against, blown up until sprites carry real physical weight. At 600 TVL the scanlines land soft and warm rather than surgical, and across a 27-inch face that is not a limitation — it is the original artistic intent, projected at full size.
Arcade-era spectacle at living-room scale — a monument that doubles as a window.

Sit a 16-bit console in front of it and the effect is immediate. Color snaps. Blacks fall away to nothing. Motion arrives with zero apology. NTSC, PAL, SECAM — it auto-detects and simply gets on with the job, the way broadcast hardware always did, no menus to negotiate and nothing to configure.

And here is the quietly great part: beneath the brute scale sits the most serviceable big CRT Sony ever made. Convergence and geometry live in a digital service menu — the finest implementation in the PVM class — so keeping the picture perfect decades on is a menu exercise rather than folklore. Machines this size usually demand rituals. This one just asks for a shelf strong enough to hold it.

## PVM-20L5
 20" multiformat

[Photo: PVM-20L5]

*PVM-20L5*

Ask around the hobby and one name keeps coming back. The 20L5 is the king of PVMs — full stop — the machine that arrived at the very end of Sony's production-monitor line with thirty years of Trinitron lessons folded into it. Plug anything into it, from any decade, and it shows why the title stuck.

The party trick is range. This is a true multiscan machine, locking anything from 15 to 33.75 kHz: a Super Nintendo at 240p, a DVD player at 480p, a broadcast feed at 1080i — same glass, same effortless lock, no option card required. One monitor that speaks every era of video fluently, which is exactly why it plays the bridge in this collection.
One monitor that speaks every era of video fluently — the bridge from 240p to HD.

At 800 TVL on SMPTE-C phosphors the picture is broadcast-honest. Colors sit precisely where the mastering engineer put them, and 240p sources take on that etched, dimensional quality only a fine-pitch HR Trinitron delivers — the look people chase for years and then refuse to give up.

The practical genius runs deeper. Inputs arrive in pairs with loop-throughs, so it drops into any chain without ceremony, and its one option slot carries a BKM-129X for SCART, VGA and RGB. ## BVM-20E1U
 20" 1000 TVL flagship

[Photo: BVM-20E1U]

*BVM-20E1U*

Every collector has one machine that justifies the whole pursuit. This is that machine. One thousand TVL, at twenty inches, in 4:3 — a number Sony hit exactly once, on exactly this chassis, and never again. A grail earns the name on a single specification.

Inside is the M49LCB22X, an aperture grille so fine — roughly a quarter of a millimeter — that even the tube in its celebrated successor is coarser. This is the sharpest large-format 4:3 glass ever to leave the company, built in an era when a master control room would clear its budget for the reference seat. Today that reference seat belongs to something better: games.
Strictly SD forever. That is not the compromise — it is the specification.

Because here is the beautiful part — it is a standard-definition instrument by design. 240p and 480i are not formats it tolerates; they are what it is for. Feed it a Saturn or a Neo Geo and the scanline definition is as sharp as the format has ever been rendered, anywhere, by anything. This is the definitive large-format 240p display, and there is no asterisk on that sentence.

It is also a machine you get to build. Four option slots wait behind the fixed RGB block, and the full E/F card family runs to eight — a whole deck of possibilities. Composite is covered, and the S-Video path runs through a BKM-24N that is already on the shelf. Half the joy of a flagship is finishing it.
The hunt is half the point.

Sightings are rare enough to count as events. A sound example surfaces perhaps once a season, then vanishes into someone's climate-controlled bay — which is what grail tier actually means: not extravagance, but patience. This one's patience traces to June 2007 build stock, still holding a picture with no living rival.

## BVM-A14F5U
 14" master grade

[Photo: BVM-A14F5U]

*BVM-A14F5U*

Every great saga needs a finale, and the A-series is how Sony's CRT story ends: one final generation, built with everything the company had learned, released into a world already turning to flat panels. The A14F5U is that finale in fourteen inches — the master-grade CRT perfected at the exact moment it became art.

It behaves like something from a later century. Beam landing correction and digital uniformity iron the image flat into the corners in a way no analog-era chassis can approach. A calibration probe hangs on the front of the glass and walks the white point to D65 by measurement rather than by eye. The monitor's entire personality — every setting, every trim — saves to a Memory Stick and travels with you.
The master-grade CRT, perfected at the exact moment it became art.

It was born to work in packs. Ethernet remote, addressing for a wall of thirty-two units, a control system designed for facilities that ran monitors the way server rooms run racks. In a home bay, all that engineering distills to one thing: total, casual command over a reference-grade picture.

And this one is nearly there. Two of the three option slots are filled: HD-SDI, and an analog board that adds SCART, component and VGA beyond anything the factory ever offered. The third slot, for a BKM-61D and its SD-SDI and S-Video inputs, is still open.

[Photo: The Confidence Wall]

Behind the tubes stands mission control. Four LMD models, nine units, one job: keep every signal honest before it touches the glass that matters. Five 9030s form the wall, two 9050s extend it into HD, a 9020 holds the analog corner, and a lone 940W speaks every modern format down to HDMI.

Flip the wall on and the appeal is immediate — identical faces lighting in sequence, one instrument with nine eyes. Run all of it at once and it still draws less power than the flagship CRT does alone.
Nine screens, one job: keep the signal honest before it reaches a tube.

The 940W is the future-proofing move: ChromaTRU color in 10-bit, one BNC that auto-detects everything from SD through 3G, HDMI for anything made this decade, waveform and audio meters built in, and a tally lamp up top — a broadcast truck condensed into four and a half pounds. In a collection built around glass, this is the crew that keeps the show running.

## Ask the bay
** “Why does 240p look sharper than 480i on the same monitor? Shouldn’t more lines win?” — Counting Lines in Louisville **The bay says**240p paints the same lines every pass, so each scanline sits still, fully lit, with black gaps that read as definition. 480i alternates half-frames sixty times a second — more information, but shimmering between two combs. Progressive stability beats interlaced quantity, which is why the sharpest thing a grail does is stand still. “What does TVL actually measure? Is 1000 TVL like 1000p?” — Static in Sacramento **The bay says**Not pixels — discernment. TVL counts how many alternating vertical lines the tube can keep separate across a width equal to the picture height. It is a measure of the glass and the grille, not the signal: feed two monitors the same 240p and the higher-TVL tube simply draws it with a finer pen. “Is composite video really that bad? It was good enough for my childhood.” — Yellow Cable Guy, Yuma **The bay says**Composite crams brightness and color down one wire and asks the monitor to untangle them — that shimmer on fine patterns is the untangling failing politely. S-Video separates the two; RGB never mixes anything at all. Your childhood was fine. Your childhood on RGB would have been a religious experience. “My PVM makes a loud THUNK when it powers on. Should I be worried?” — First-Time Tuber, Tustin **The bay says**That is the degauss coil firing — a deliberate magnetic pulse that wipes the shadow mask clean of stray fields so the colors land pure. It is not a fault; it is the monitor clearing its throat. Worry on the day it stops.

### Speak broadcast

- **TVL**: How many vertical lines the tube can keep separate across a width equal to the height. Bigger number, sharper brag.
- **15 kHz**: The heartbeat of standard definition — the sweep rate every retro console speaks natively.
- **Aperture grille**: Trinitron’s vertical wire mask. The reason the blacks are black and the stripes are famous.
- **SMPTE-C**: The broadcast phosphor standard. Colors exactly where the mastering engineer left them.
- **Loop-through**: The monitor passes the signal along untouched, like a good bartender.
- **Multiscan**: Locks to many sweep rates instead of one. The difference between a specialist and the 20L5.
- **ISR**: Sony’s serial remote protocol — one controller, a wall of monitors, total command.
- **Degauss**: The THUNK at power-on. It is demagnetizing the mask, not planning anything.

title: The Signal Chain: Consoles to Sony Pro Monitors
description: How a shelf of retro consoles reaches a fleet of Sony professional monitors: SCART switchers, BNC runs, a distribution amp, and why there is no scaler anywhere.
text:
The Setup

# How the Signal Gets to the Glass

A shelf of consoles, thirteen Sony professional monitors, and not one scaler in the building. Here is the actual path a picture takes from a cartridge to a broadcast tube — cable by cable, box by box.

Every article about professional monitors, this site's included, spends its time on *why*: why RGB beats composite, why a BVM shows you the truth. Almost none of them tell you *how* — what you actually buy, what plugs into what, and what happens when you try to put eight consoles on two screens. That gap is the reason a lot of people own one PVM and one modded console and still have them sitting in different rooms.

So here is the whole thing, unglamorous parts included. Two rooms, two nearly identical chains, and one deliberate omission that shapes everything else.
 **The house rule:** nothing gets processed. No upscaler, no line doubler, no frame buffer — no OSSC, no RetroTINK, no Framemeister anywhere in the signal path. A CRT is the one display that wants exactly what these consoles put out: 240p, 15kHz, analog RGB, warts and all. Every box you insert to "improve" that is a box making decisions on your behalf, and adding a frame or two of lag while it thinks. The whole point of the fleet is to not need one.

## The chain, end to end

### Game room

Eight consoles, two big PVMs, one switcher doing all the work.
 **The consoles**Saturn, Genesis, SNES, N64, PC Engine and friends — each on its own RGB SCART cable ▸ **GSCARTSW v5.2**8 in, 2 out. Auto-switching: power on a console and it takes the screen ▸ **PVM-2950Q**29-inch, via SCART → 4 BNC **PVM-20L5**20-inch multiformat, same cable type

### Garage arcade — the broadcast pair

The same idea again, in the room where the serious glass lives.
 **The consoles**Garage-side machines, RGB SCART again ▸ **Second GSCARTSW**Its own switcher, so neither room borrows from the other ▸ **BVM-20E1U**The primary E-series chassis **BVM-A14F5U**Two of three card slots filled

### Garage arcade — the LMD wall

A completely separate system, and the one people ask about first.
 **Receiver + USB stick**Looping video, plus a PS2 on a switcher when someone wants to play ▸ **CE Labs AV901-HD**1 in, 9 out component distribution amp — unity gain, 75 ohm ▸ **The LMD squadron**Every LMD in the rack showing the same picture at the same instant

## The switcher is the whole trick

The single component that makes a collection this size usable is the **GSCARTSW** — an eight-input, two-output RGB SCART switcher, and there is one in each room. Eight consoles stay permanently plugged in. It auto-switches: power on the Saturn and the Saturn takes the screen, no button, no menu, no crawling behind a rack. That sounds like a convenience feature. It is actually the difference between a collection you play and a collection you look at.

Two outputs, two monitors, one per screen. That is why each room has its own switcher rather than one big one feeding the house — a second unit is cheaper than the cable run, and it means the garage never has to wait for the game room.
 **If you are building your own:** buy the switcher before you buy the second console. Everyone does this in the wrong order — they accumulate machines, run out of inputs, and end up swapping cables until they stop bothering. A good auto-switcher is the thing that keeps hardware in rotation.

## SCART goes in, BNC comes out

Here is the join that trips people up. The console world speaks **SCART** — a fat European connector carrying RGB and audio in one plug. The Sony professional world speaks **BNC** — individual coaxial connectors, one per signal, twist-locked, because a broadcast engineer is not interested in a cable that can fall out. A PVM has no SCART socket and never will.

The bridge is a **SCART to 4 BNC breakout cable** — red, green, blue and sync on four BNCs, with an audio pair broken out alongside. The ones in use here come in both male and female SCART variants, depending on which end of the chain they land on. That single cable type is what makes the whole collection possible; without it the two halves of this hobby simply do not connect.

Sync goes straight through. No stripper, no LM1881, no sync-on-green workaround — the composite sync riding on the SCART cable goes into the monitor's sync BNC as-is, and these monitors lock onto it without complaint. Professional Sony gear is far less fussy about sync than internet folklore suggests.

## The audio nobody plans for

The AMS-100s sitting on top of the monitors are not decoration. They are fed from the same breakout cables — the audio pair that comes off the SCART side, running into the audio monitor rather than into the CRT's small internal speaker. It is the correct period arrangement, it is how a real edit bay was laid out, and it sounds dramatically better than any CRT speaker ever did.

This is the part most home setups skip, and it is worth not skipping. You go to enormous trouble to get the video signal pristine, then listen to it through a two-inch driver behind a metal grille. The audio path deserves the same attention as the video one.

## The wall is a different animal

The LMD rack does not run on any of the above. It is component video, not RGB SCART, and it is fed from a single source through a **CE Labs AV901-HD** distribution amplifier — one input, nine outputs, unity gain into 75 ohm terminations. A distribution amp is not a splitter; a passive splitter halves your signal every time it divides, and by the ninth monitor there would be nothing left. A DA buffers and re-drives, so the last screen in the chain looks like the first.

What feeds it is deliberately mundane: a receiver playing video off a USB stick, with a PS2 switchable in when someone wants to actually play something. The effect is the point — every LMD in the rack showing the same frame at the same instant, which is precisely what these monitors did in the machine rooms they came from.

## The cabinets are not part of any of this

Worth saying plainly, because it is the question that follows: none of the arcade cabinets touch the switchers, the breakout cables or the distribution amp. Each one is a closed, original system — its board drives its own monitor inside its own cabinet, the way it left the factory. They are not all JAMMA and they were never rewired to feed the rack.

That is deliberate. A cabinet that has been opened up and re-plumbed into a modern signal path is a cabinet that has stopped being the thing it was. The monitor fleet exists to serve the consoles; the cabinets serve themselves.

## What it costs you

Honesty about the trade: this setup is analog end to end, which means it is fussy in ways a modern one is not. Cables are specific and mostly not available at retail. Every console needs the right RGB cable for that console, and some of them need modding before they output RGB at all — the NES never did officially, which is why the top loader here carries an NESRGB board. Nothing here will ever appear on a flat panel without adding exactly the kind of box this setup refuses to use.

What you get in return is a picture with nothing between the console and the tube, and a room where you press a power button and a game is on screen a second later. For a collection meant to be played rather than displayed, that trade has never once looked like the wrong one.

Curious what the monitors on the other end of these cables actually are? PVM vs. BVM (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-vs-bvm.html) covers the difference, and the fleet roster (https://www.orlandu.com/monitors.html) lists every unit. The consoles doing the sending are on the consoles page (https://www.orlandu.com/consoles.html).

title: How to Connect a Retro Console to a Sony PVM or BVM
description: What plugs into what to get a retro console onto a Sony PVM or BVM: the RGB cable, the switcher, the SCART to 4 BNC breakout, sync, termination and audio.
text:
How-To

# How to Connect a Retro Console to a Sony PVM or BVM

A PVM has no SCART socket, no HDMI, and no interest in making this easy. Here is what actually plugs into what — the cable, the switcher, the four BNCs — and the one box you do not need.

Every article about professional monitors, this site's included, spends its time on why. This one is the how, written from a setup that runs eight consoles into thirteen Sony monitors with no scaler anywhere in the path. Nothing in it is exotic. The whole trick is four cables and one switch.

## 1. Start with RGB out of the console

A professional monitor wants red, green and blue as separate signals, which is what these consoles make internally. Some put it on the back connector from the factory; some need a board. Here is how the consoles in this collection got there.

| Console | RGB out of the box? | What it took here |
|---|---|---|
| Super Nintendo | Yes, native | The right RGB SCART cable and nothing else |
| Sega Genesis Model 1 | Yes, native | An RGB SCART cable; S-Video and stereo jacks were added later, separately |
| Sega Genesis CDX | Yes, native | An RGB SCART cable |
| Sega Saturn | Yes, native | An RGB SCART cable |
| NES, front loader and top loader | No | An NESRGB board in each |
| Nintendo 64 | No | An RGB upgrade |
| PC Engine Duo-R | No | An RGB mod, alongside the region mod |
| GameCube | No RGB | Component over the OEM component cable |
| PlayStation 2 | No RGB | Component |

If your console is not on the list, the question is the same one: does it output RGB natively, and if not, which board gets it there. The full console table → (https://www.orlandu.com/consoles.html#mods)

## 2. The right RGB SCART cable for that console

The console world speaks SCART — RGB and audio in one fat connector. One cable per console, and "RGB SCART" on the label is not enough: each machine has its own pinout and its own needs, so the cable has to be built for the console it plugs into. The same cable carries the console's sound and its sync, and both matter two steps from now.

## 3. A switcher, if you own more than one console

A GSCARTSW — eight inputs, two outputs, auto-switching. Power on a console and it takes the screen; no button, no menu, no crawling behind a rack. Two outputs means two monitors.

Buy the switcher before you buy the second console.

Everyone does this in the wrong order — they accumulate machines, run out of inputs, and end up swapping cables until they stop bothering. A good auto-switcher is the thing that keeps hardware in rotation.

## 4. SCART in, four BNCs out

The bridge is a SCART to 4 BNC breakout cable: red, green, blue and sync on four BNCs, with the audio pair broken out alongside. They come male and female, depending on which end of the chain they land on. On the monitor, those four go to the BNCs labeled R, G, B and EXT SYNC.

Sync goes straight through — the composite sync riding the SCART cable into the sync BNC as-is, no stripper, no LM1881, no sync-on-green workaround. These monitors lock onto it without complaint; professional Sony gear is far less fussy about sync than internet folklore suggests.

Two things to set on the monitor. Professional inputs loop through to feed the next monitor in a chain, so the last monitor on the line — or the only one — needs its 75 Ω termination switched on, or the picture washes out. And on a monitor whose BNCs accept both RGB and component, the PVM-20L5 among them, the input has to be told it is looking at RGB.

## 5. Component sources skip the switcher

The GameCube and the PlayStation 2 go component, over the OEM cable, into the monitor's component input — on a BVM-A through its analog option card, on a PVM-20L5 the same BNCs. Here the PS2 feeds a wall of nine LMDs through a distribution amplifier, which is not a splitter: a splitter halves the signal every time it divides, a DA buffers and re-drives it. The full chain, both rooms → (https://www.orlandu.com/signal-chain.html)

## 6. The audio nobody plans for

The breakout's audio pair goes to a powered monitor speaker, not the two-inch driver behind the CRT's grille. Here it is the AMS-100 on top of each monitor — how a real edit bay was laid out, and how it should sound. You go to enormous trouble to get the video signal pristine; the audio path deserves the same attention.

## 7. What you do not need

No upscaler, no line doubler, no frame buffer — no OSSC, no RetroTINK, no Framemeister. A CRT is the one display that wants exactly what these consoles put out: 240p, 15 kHz, analog RGB, warts and all. Every box you add between them makes decisions on your behalf and adds lag while it thinks. The whole point of a professional monitor is to not need one.

## Quick answers

### Can I plug a SCART cable straight into a PVM?

No. A PVM has no SCART socket and never will. The SCART to 4 BNC breakout is the bridge — red, green, blue and sync on four BNCs, audio alongside.

### Do I need a sync stripper?

Not in this experience. Composite sync goes from the SCART cable straight into the sync BNC, and every console on the list above locks without a stripper, an LM1881 or a sync-on-green workaround.

### Which consoles output RGB without a mod?

Of the ones here: the Super Nintendo, the Genesis, the Genesis CDX and the Saturn. The NES, the Nintendo 64 and the PC Engine needed boards.

### Will a BVM take the same cables?

Yes — the same breakout, the same four BNCs. On the E/F series they land on the fixed input block; on the A series, on an analog option card. PVM vs. BVM → (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-vs-bvm.html)

### What about composite or S-Video?

Most PVMs take both, and a BVM decodes them through a card. But the picture is the reason you bought the monitor, and composite is not it.

Buying the monitor first? What to check before you buy a PVM-20L5 (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-20l5-buying-guide.html) is the sweep, and the field guide (https://www.orlandu.com/crt-field-guide.html) is how to spot one in the wild.

title: PVM vs. BVM: Sony's Pro Monitors Explained
description: Why the best screens for retro games were never sold to gamers: how Sony's PVM and BVM professional monitors differ, and which one you actually want.
text:
Did You Know?

# The Best Screen for Retro Games Was Never Sold to Gamers

The monitors in this collection weren't made for living rooms. They were made for broadcast engineers — and that's exactly why retro games have never looked better on anything else.

While consumers were buying Trinitrons at the mall, Sony was quietly selling a different class of CRT out the back door — professional monitors, built for television studios, edit bays, and master control rooms, at prices that would have made a Best Buy shopper faint. They came in two main families, and the letters on the badge tell you everything: **PVM**, the Professional Video Monitor, and **BVM**, the Broadcast Video Monitor.

The PVM was the workhorse. Studios used them for previewing feeds, hospitals wired them to imaging equipment, security desks stacked them in walls. Compared to a consumer TV, a PVM has a finer aperture grille, far higher line resolution, and — the part that matters most to game collectors — direct RGB input. A consumer TV of the era took a composite signal, a single muddy wire where the colors have already been smeared together. A PVM takes red, green, and blue as separate signals, straight from the console's video chip, nothing lost in translation. Plug a Genesis or a Super Nintendo into one over RGB and the image snaps into focus like someone cleaned a window you didn't know was dirty.

The BVM was something else entirely: Sony's reference grade, the monitors broadcast engineers used to judge whether the picture itself was correct. Hand-selected tubes, modular input cards (the BKM cards hunted on the wanted list (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html)), calibration controls deep enough to get lost in, and new prices that ran well into five figures — for a monitor a viewer at home would never see. A BVM doesn't try to make the picture pretty. It shows you the truth, scanline by scanline. For pixel art drawn by hand in the '80s and '90s, the truth turns out to be gorgeous.

[Photo: Sonic and Knuckles running on two Sony BVM broadcast monitors, an AMS-100 audio monitor riding on top of each]

***Sonic & Knuckles, broadcast grade** — the BVM pair on the workbench, AMS-100s riding on top*

## PVM vs. BVM at a glance

| | PVM — Professional Video Monitor | BVM — Broadcast Video Monitor |
|---|---|---|
| Job | Production — previewing feeds in studios, edit bays, hospitals, security walls | Reference — the seat where an engineer judged whether the picture itself was correct |
| Resolution | 600–800 TV lines (PVM-2950Q (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-2950q.html) 600, PVM-20L5 (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-20l5.html) 800) | 800–1,000 TV lines (BVM-A14F5U (https://www.orlandu.com/bvm-a14f5u.html) 800, BVM-20E1U (https://www.orlandu.com/bvm-20e1u.html) 1,000 — a number Sony hit once) |
| Tube | Trinitron or HR Trinitron | HR Trinitron, hand-selected; E-grade on the 20E1U |
| Inputs | Fixed on the back panel: RGB/component BNCs, composite, S-Video; one option slot on the late 20L5 | Modular BKM cards in 3–4 slots; the E/F series keeps one fixed RGB block, the A series has no analog input at all until a card is fitted |
| Formats | 15 kHz standard definition on most (the 2950Q: NTSC, PAL, SECAM); the late 20L5 is multiscan, 240p to 1080i | Model by model: strictly SD on the E/F series (240p, 480i, 576i); 240p to 1080i and 24PsF on the A series |
| Calibration | Front-panel picture controls | Deep — beam-landing correction, digital uniformity, a probe that walks the white point to D65 on the A series |
| Weight | PVM-20L5 ≈73 lb; PVM-2950Q 115 lb | BVM-20E1U ≈85 lb; BVM-A14F5U ≈48 lb |
| For a game collector | The right answer for most — the picture gap to a BVM is small | The sharpest 240p ever rendered (the 20E1U), or reference work |

The fleet here — thirteen units across eight models, documented in Trinitron Fleet, Vol. 1 (https://www.orlandu.com/trinitron-fleet-vol1.html) — grew out of a single purchase more than a decade ago: a 13-inch PVM-1354Q. One good monitor is a slippery slope; that first PVM has since moved on, the way first monitors do, but it opened the door to everything on the Monitor Fleet page (https://www.orlandu.com/monitors.html).

One good monitor is a slippery slope.

Asked to pick just one to recommend today, the answer from this garage is the **PVM-20L5** (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-20l5-buying-guide.html) — a late-generation 20-inch multiformat unit that handles nearly anything you feed it, big enough to matter, versatile enough to be the only monitor you need. The sentimental pick is different: the **PVM-2950Q**, the 29-inch cube in the game room. It's an unreasonable object — enormous, heavy, shaped like a monolith — and Super Mario Bros. on that much curved glass is a religious experience. Versatility is a reason to buy a monitor. The 2950Q is a reason to keep one.

## Quick answers

### What is the difference between a PVM and a BVM?

Grade. A PVM is Sony's production monitor — the workhorse a studio used to preview a feed. A BVM is the reference monitor — the seat where an engineer judged whether the picture itself was correct, with hand-selected tubes, modular BKM input cards, calibration depth a PVM was never given, and up to 1,000 TV lines against a PVM's 600 to 800. Both take RGB, and both leave any consumer TV far behind.

### Is a BVM better than a PVM for retro games?

Sharper, yes. But the gap between a well-set-up PVM and a BVM is far smaller than the gap between either of them and anything sold in a store. For 240p the BVM-20E1U is the definitive large-format display; for a collection that runs from 240p to HD, a multiformat PVM-20L5 covers more ground than most BVMs. Most collectors are well served by a PVM.

### Do PVMs and BVMs take RGB from a console?

Yes — direct RGB is the point of both. A PVM carries RGB/component BNCs on its back panel; a BVM takes RGB through a fixed input block on the E/F series or an option card on the A series. A console reaches either over an RGB SCART cable and a SCART to 4 BNC breakout cable — the chain this collection runs → (https://www.orlandu.com/signal-chain.html)

### What are BKM cards?

Sony's plug-in input boards for BVMs, and for the single option slot on late PVMs: decoders for composite and S-Video, SDI and HD-SDI inputs, analog RGB and component. A BVM is only as useful as the cards in it, which is why the hunt for them has a standing entry on the wanted list (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html). (Glossary → (https://www.orlandu.com/glossary.html#bkm))

### Which Sony professional monitor should a collector buy first?

From this garage, the PVM-20L5: 800 TV lines, multiscan from 240p to 1080i, one option slot, and versatile enough to be the only monitor you need. There is a full pre-purchase checklist for it here → (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-20l5-buying-guide.html)

Sitting on professional Sony gear you don't want to freight across the country? The arcade buys — and when the fleet consolidates, departures land on the For Sale page (https://www.orlandu.com/forsale.html). Email orlandusarcade@gmail.com.

title: How to Spot Professional Glass in the Wild
description: How to recognize a Sony professional monitor at a thrift store or estate sale — the badge, the BNC tells, the lookalikes and the thirty-second check.
text:
Field Guide

# How to Spot Professional Glass in the Wild

The best screens ever pointed at a video game are still out there — in estate garages, station clean-outs, university surplus auctions, and the back row of a thrift store's electronics shelf, priced like old TVs by people who think that's what they are. Telling a professional monitor from a heavy consumer set takes about five minutes to learn. Here are the five minutes.

## Read the badge first

A consumer set shouts TRINITRON across its face. A professional monitor states a model number, in small type, and lets you do the math: PVM-2030, BVM-14F5U, LMD-9050. The letters are the family — **PVM** for Professional Video Monitor, **BVM** for Broadcast Video Monitor, **LMD** for the flat-panel generation that followed — and the leading digits are usually the tube size. A PVM-20L5 is a twenty-inch; a BVM-14F5U is a fourteen.

If the thing in front of you has a tuner, it’s a TV. If it has a button labeled LINE or RGB, keep reading.

The front panel confirms it. A television has a channel display, a volume control, maybe a cabinet speaker grille. A monitor has a row of input-select buttons, a handful of small setup controls, and no interest in entertaining you. If the thing in front of you has a tuner, it's a TV. If it has a button labeled *LINE* or *RGB*, keep reading.

## No badge? Read the back

The rear panel is where a professional monitor stops pretending. Instead of a couple of RCA jacks, you'll find rows of **BNC connectors** — the twist-lock coaxial fittings broadcast gear uses, one per signal, because an engineer is not interested in a cable that can fall out. They often come in pairs, because professional inputs loop through to feed the next monitor in the chain. Add a steel chassis, real handles or rack ears, and no antenna input anywhere, and you're looking at something that was bolted into a facility, not parked in a living room.

## What the letters actually buy

The PVM was the workhorse — studios previewed feeds on them, hospitals wired them to imaging carts, security desks stacked them into walls. The BVM was the reference grade: hand-selected tubes, modular input cards, and new prices that ran well into five figures, for judging whether the picture itself was correct. Both take RGB straight from a console's video chip, which is why retro games have never looked better on anything else. The full story of the two families — and which one to actually buy — is in PVM vs. BVM (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-vs-bvm.html).

## Not every PVM is a jackpot

The line ran for decades, from small security-desk units to the late multiformat machines, and the value follows the inputs and the tube. Check the back for a group of BNCs labeled **R, G and B** — direct RGB input is most of what makes these monitors matter to game collectors. A composite-only unit is still a well-built monitor; it is not the find. And look at what's riding in the option slot, if the chassis has one: the plug-in input cards are their own market, and some of them are actively hunted — a few are on the wanted list here (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html).

## The thirty-second check when it can't be powered

Most field finds can't be plugged in on the spot, and you can still learn plenty. Check the plastics — bezel tabs, handles, vent slots — because cracks there are forever. Look at the tube face under raking light: scratches, and the ghost of whatever the monitor spent years displaying, both show on dead glass. Check the chassis and rear for rust and water staining. Count what's missing — knobs, buttons, the option-slot cover — because small Sony parts are their own hunt.

## If it powers up

Then you run the real sweep: a geometry grid corner to corner, a white field, a black field in a dim room, every input one at a time. The whole ritual is written up in the PVM-20L5 buying guide (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-20l5-buying-guide.html) and condensed onto a printable one-page checklist (https://www.orlandu.com/media/pvm-20l5-checklist.pdf) — the guide is about one monitor, but the sweep works on any of them.

## Worth hauling?

Decide by weight class before you lift. A nine-inch rides in a passenger seat; a twenty-inch is a two-person carry; the big tubes are furniture that happens to glow, and every pound of it is glass and copper that does not forgive being dropped. Bring a blanket, keep the tube face away from anything hard, and never ship one you could drive to instead.
 9-inchRides in a passenger seat20-inchA two-person carryThe big tubesFurniture that happens to glow

And when in doubt — take it. Professional glass has stopped being made forever, the supply only shrinks, and the worst case is that you own a spare for a machine the hobby will absolutely absorb. The people who regret these purchases are, almost without exception, the ones who left it on the shelf.

The people who regret these purchases are, almost without exception, the ones who left it on the shelf.

## Quick answers

### How do I know if a CRT is a professional monitor?

Read the badge: a model number in small type — PVM-, BVM-, LMD- — instead of TRINITRON across the face. No tuner, input-select buttons instead of channel controls, and rows of BNC connectors on the back, often in loop-through pairs.

### What do PVM, BVM and LMD stand for?

Professional Video Monitor, Broadcast Video Monitor, and the flat-panel line that followed. The leading digits are usually the tube size: a PVM-20L5 is a twenty-inch, a BVM-14F5U a fourteen.

### Is every PVM worth buying?

No. Value follows the inputs and the tube. Look for a group of BNCs labeled R, G and B — direct RGB input is most of what makes these monitors matter to game collectors. A composite-only unit is a well-built monitor, not the find. Check what's riding in the option slot, if there is one.

### What can I check if it can't be powered on?

The plastics (bezel tabs, handles, vent slots — cracks are forever), the tube face under raking light for scratches and the ghost of what it displayed for years, the chassis and rear for rust and water staining, and what's missing: knobs, buttons, the option-slot cover.

### How heavy are they?

A nine-inch rides in a passenger seat; a twenty-inch is a two-person carry; the big tubes are furniture that happens to glow. Bring a blanket, and never ship one you could drive to.

Found professional Sony gear you don't want to keep — or can't identify? The arcade buys, and identifying mystery hardware is half the fun. Email a photo: orlandusarcade@gmail.com.
