title: PVM-20L5 Buying Guide: What to Check
description: What to look for when buying a Sony PVM-20L5: the one check that tells you most, judging a tube with no hours counter, what to pay, and why not to ship one.
text:
Buyer's Guide

# What to Check Before You Buy a PVM-20L5

Ask around the hobby long enough and the same monitor keeps coming back. Here is what actually matters when you are standing in front of one — and what to do about the fact that you probably should not ship it.

The PVM-20L5 arrived at the end of Sony's production-monitor line with three decades of Trinitron lessons folded into it, and the reputation it earned has not faded. The case for it is not nostalgia. It is range. This is a true multiscan chassis, locking anything from about 15 to 33.75 kHz: a Super Nintendo at 240p, a DVD player at 480p, a broadcast feed at 1080i — same glass, same effortless lock, no option card required. At 800 TV lines on a fine-pitch HR Trinitron tube with SMPTE-C phosphors, the picture is broadcast-honest. One monitor that speaks every era of video fluently is a rare thing, and it is why this one plays the bridge in this collection.
 15–33.75 kHzScan range800 TV linesHR Trinitron, SMPTE-C73 lbA two-person lift

It is also twenty-odd years old, weighs about seventy-three pounds, and there is no warranty department left to call. So before money changes hands, here is the sweep.

Print the one-page PVM-20L5 pre-purchase checklist (PDF) → (https://www.orlandu.com/media/pvm-20l5-checklist.pdf) — the whole sweep condensed to a single sheet, made to ride along to the seller's garage.

[Photo: Sony PVM-20L5 professional monitor lit and running Super Mario Sunshine, an AMS-100 audio monitor on top]

***The 20L5 in place** — AMS-100 on top, *Super Mario Sunshine* at 480p*

## How close is it to a BVM?

Closer than the badge suggests, and that is most of why this monitor holds its price. The 20L5 borrows the parts of the broadcast playbook that actually matter. Its option slot takes BKM cards from the same modular family the BVMs use, so the input side is expandable rather than frozen at whatever shipped on the back panel. Its phosphors are SMPTE-C, the broadcast color standard, which is why color lands where the mastering engineer put it instead of where a consumer set thinks it should be. And the parts lineage runs deep enough that the flyback is shared with the BVM-D14H5 — the kind of commonality that keeps a twenty-year-old monitor serviceable long after the line shut down.

Where it stops short is grade. A BVM (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-vs-bvm.html) is a reference instrument: 1000 TV lines against the 20L5's 800, hand-selected tubes, and calibration depth a production monitor was never given. If the job is judging whether a picture is correct, that is still a BVM's job and no PVM substitutes for it.

But that is not the job most people are buying one for. For playing games on, the distance between a well-set-up 20L5 and a BVM is far smaller than the distance between either of them and anything that was ever sold in a store — and the 20L5 does it across a range of formats no single BVM of the era touches. That is the trade, and for most buyers it is the right side of it.

## Start with a grid

If you only get to do one thing, put a corner-to-corner geometry grid on the screen. Nothing else tells you as much as fast. Geometry and convergence are the expensive problems on a monitor like this — the ones that mean a service bench, a specialist, and a bill — and a grid puts every one of them in plain sight at once.

Look down the lines, not at them.

Look down the lines, not at them. Are the verticals actually vertical at the far left and far right, or do they bow? Is the spacing even from edge to edge, or are the boxes on one side stretched wider than the boxes on the other? Do the red, green and blue fringes separate in the corners? A little convergence drift in the extreme corners is normal on a tube this age and adjustable. Lines that bend, or a picture that is visibly wider on one side than the other, is a different conversation.

Bring your own source. A seller's hookup tells you what the seller wants you to see; a pattern you brought tells you what is there. The one used here is the 240p Test Suite (https://github.com/ArtemioUrbina/240pTestSuite) — Artemio Urbina's homebrew, which exists as a ROM or disc image for a long list of consoles, from the NES and Super Nintendo through the Genesis, PC Engine, Saturn, Dreamcast and GameCube. Whichever machine is easiest to carry is the one that can carry it, and it puts a proper grid on the screen instead of whatever the seller happened to leave paused.

## Then the rest of the sweep

- **Full white field** — purity, uniformity and blotching all show up at once. Watch the corners for color casts and the center for dimness.
- **Full black in a dim room** — retrace lines, glow, and a badly set screen control give themselves away instantly.
- **A real 240p source** — scanline structure and how cleanly it locks. This is what you are buying it for, so test it.
- **Every input, one at a time** — composite, S-Video, the RGB/component BNCs, and whatever is in the option slot. A dead input is easy to hide behind a working one.
- **The front panel** — every button and every pot. Scratchy controls and dead buttons are common and annoying.
- **The plastics** — bezel tabs, the handles, the vent slots. Cracks here are forever.
- **The chassis and rear** — rust, water staining, evidence of a hard life in a rack or a damp garage.
- **How it comes up cold** — ask to see it switched on from cold, then again after half an hour. Some faults only appear at one end of that.

## The faults people talk about

Three problems come up whenever this monitor is discussed: the power section on the G board, horizontal linearity on early serials, and brittle plastics. Worth knowing, worth checking for — and worth being straight about where that list comes from. **It is the hobby's collective experience, not this bench.** The unit here has shown none of the three, and there is no reliable serial cutoff for the linearity issue that this garage can point to. Treat all three as things to look for, not as things that will happen.

## Judging a tube with no numbers

The 20L5 does not hand you an hours counter. There is no number to read, no total to compare, nothing to screenshot for a listing. You are judging it by eye, which sounds worse than it is once you know what you are looking at.

A tired tube tells on itself. Whites go dull and slightly warm rather than clean. The picture looks washed instead of deep, and blacks sit gray. Most tellingly, it needs help to reach normal brightness — if the screen control has been run up high just to get an ordinary picture, someone has been compensating for a tube that is giving up. Ask what the settings were before you arrived, and be suspicious of a monitor delivered with brightness and contrast already near maximum.

## The card question

The 20L5 has one option slot, and what is in it changes what the monitor is worth to you. A unit that already carries the right input card is worth more than the same monitor plus that card bought separately, because the cards are their own hunt — they surface irregularly, they are priced by people who know exactly what they have, and they are the reason there is a standing entry on the wanted list (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html) here. If a listing includes a card, weigh it properly instead of treating it as a bonus.

## What to pay

One number here is worth quoting with any confidence: a clean, all-original unit with a good input card sits in the **$2,800 – $3,500** range, and examples have traded at the top of it. Below that the market moves too much — condition, luck, and how badly a seller wants the space back — for a figure from this garage to be worth much. So the rest is relative. Verify all of it against current eBay sold listings before you make an offer: sold, not asking, and the gap between those two is where most disappointment lives.

| Condition | Where it sits | What that means |
|---|---|---|
| Untested or needs work | A fraction of a clean example | Sold as-is, unknown hours, or a known fault. You are buying a project and a heavy one. |
| Working, cosmetically tired | Well under a clean example | Good picture, scuffed case, no card. The honest middle of the market. |
| Clean and working, no card | Below the top band — the card is a real part of that gap | Strong tube, tidy geometry, plastics intact. |
| Excellent, all original, with a good input card | $2,800 – $3,500 | The one you keep. Rare enough that the price holds. |

## Do not ship it

This is the strongest opinion in this guide. Plenty of people ship these monitors and some of them arrive fine. The recommendation from here is still don't. Seventy-three pounds of glass, a heavy chassis, and a tube neck that does not forgive a hard drop is not a parcel. It is freight that happens to be shaped like a box.

Seventy-three pounds of glass, a heavy chassis, and a tube neck that does not forgive a hard drop is not a parcel.

The only exception worth making is a freight company that will wrap it properly and insure it for what it is actually worth — not a carrier's flat declared value, and not a seller promising they are good at packing. If those two conditions are not both met, walk away from the listing and keep looking closer to home. A monitor that arrives with a cracked bezel or a dead tube is not a bargain that went slightly wrong; it is a total loss with shipping charges attached.

Which means the real advice is simpler than it sounds: buy one you can drive to. Bring a friend, bring a moving blanket, and bring a grid.

## Where to look

- **Facebook Marketplace and local classifieds** — the cheapest route and the one that fits driving distance. Marketplace especially: set the radius as wide as you are willing to drive, save the search, and let it work. It rewards patience and a saved alert more than it rewards effort.
- **The forums** — KLOV, Arcade-Projects, the shmups community. Sellers who know what they have, describe it accurately, and understand why you want to collect it in person.
- **eBay, filtered to local pickup only** — eBay's reach without eBay's shipping risk. Sort by distance and check it often.
- **Broadcast and AV liquidations** — station cleanouts, production house closures, university AV departments. Where these came from originally, and still the best odds on a unit that was maintained.

## When it is the wrong monitor

It is a great monitor. It is not automatically the right one for you, and the multiscan range is exactly where that turns.

If everything you own outputs 240p — an NES, a Super Nintendo, a Genesis, a shelf of the same — you are paying a premium for a span of frequencies you will never reach. A cheaper 20-inch PVM shows 240p beautifully and leaves money in your pocket for the RGB cables and the switcher that will actually change how it looks. Buy the 20L5 when the range is the point: when a DVD player, a component source and an HD feed all need to land on the same glass.

And if the goal is critical HD reference work rather than games, this is the wrong family entirely. That is a BVM conversation, and there is a whole piece here on the difference (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-vs-bvm.html).

Whichever way that lands, know what you are signing up for. Seventy-three pounds is a two-person lift and a real footprint. It runs hot and it wants air. It is past twenty years old, there is no factory support behind it, and the number of people who can competently service one is shrinking rather than growing. None of that is a reason not to buy one. All of it is a reason to buy the best example you can find rather than the cheapest.

## Quick answers

### What resolutions does the PVM-20L5 accept?

It is a true multiscan monitor, locking roughly 15 to 33.75 kHz: 240p and 480i from retro consoles, 480p from a DVD player or GameCube, and 1080i from a broadcast feed — all on the same tube, with no option card required. That range is the reason to buy this one over a cheaper 20-inch PVM.

### How does the PVM-20L5 compare to a BVM?

It borrows the parts of the broadcast playbook that matter — a BKM option slot, SMPTE-C phosphors, a flyback shared with the BVM-D14H5 — but it is 800 TV lines to a BVM's 1000, without the hand-selected tubes or calibration depth. For games the gap is small; for judging whether a picture is correct, it is still a BVM's job. The full comparison → (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-vs-bvm.html)

### Which BKM card does the PVM-20L5 take?

One option slot, from the same modular BKM family the BVMs use. The unit here runs a BKM-129X, which adds SCART, VGA and RGB. A monitor sold with the right card is worth more than the same monitor plus that card bought separately — the cards are their own hunt.

### Can a PVM-20L5 be shipped?

The advice here is don't. Seventy-three pounds of glass and a tube neck that does not forgive a hard drop is freight, not a parcel. The only exception is a freight company that wraps it properly and insures it for what it is actually worth. Otherwise, buy one you can drive to.

### Is the PVM-20L5 worth it for 240p-only consoles?

Probably not. If everything you own is an NES, Super Nintendo or Genesis, you are paying a premium for frequencies you will never reach, and a cheaper 20-inch PVM shows 240p beautifully. Buy the 20L5 when the range is the point — a DVD player, a component source and an HD feed on the same glass.

## One last thing

Do not wait. The 20L5 has been quietly appreciating for years and there is no manufacturing line to relieve the pressure. Every clean one that sells makes the next clean one dearer. If you find a good example within driving distance at a fair number, the mistake is almost never buying it — it is the six months you spend deciding, watching the price of the thing you already wanted go up.

One more place to look: the For Sale page here (https://www.orlandu.com/forsale.html) — the collection consolidates over time, and monitors that leave get listed. And if you have a 20L5 — or any professional Sony — you'd rather sell than ship, the arcade buys and knows exactly what it's looking at: orlandusarcade@gmail.com.

How to cite: Orlandu’s Arcade (“Orlandu81”), *What to Check Before You Buy a PVM-20L5*, orlandu.com, 2026, https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-20l5-buying-guide.html

title: VS. Super Mario Bros.: The Arcade Original
description: VS. Super Mario Bros. looks like the NES game everyone knows — it isn't. How Nintendo's arcade version became the hardest Super Mario Bros. of them all.
text:
Did You Know?

# The Hardest Super Mario Bros. Most People Never Noticed

The VS. UniSystem runs VS. Super Mario Bros. — and if you think that's the game you mastered on your NES, the machine would like a word.

In March 1986, about a year after Super Mario Bros. conquered living rooms, Nintendo brought Mario back to the arcades on its VS. System hardware. At a glance, VS. Super Mario Bros. looks identical to the NES game — same physics, same music, same World 1-1 opening. That resemblance was the trap. Nintendo knew that a game you could finish on one quarter doesn't earn its keep in an arcade, so under the familiar surface they quietly rebuilt the game to fight back.

The changes start small and get mean. The hidden 1-Up Mushrooms in worlds 2-1, 4-1, 6-1, and 8-1? Gone entirely — and the ones that remain only appear if you've collected enough coins in the preceding levels. The famous infinite-lives turtle trick on the staircase? Patched, decades before "patch" was a word players knew: the Koopas and Buzzy Beetles on those stairs were swapped for Goombas, which can't be bounced. Even the Minus World glitch was partly bricked over. Extra lives now cost 100 to 250 coins on a new three-digit counter, and operators could set the machine to start you with two lives instead of three.

Then there are the levels themselves. Many of the easier NES stages were swapped out for crueler variants — 2-2, for instance, becomes the notoriously tricky 7-2 layout. More enemies, more bottomless pits, fewer and less generous power-up blocks throughout. And six levels in VS. Super Mario Bros. were entirely new — designs that players outside Japan wouldn't see again until they surfaced in Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels, the Japanese Super Mario Bros. 2 that Nintendo of America famously deemed too hard for release. American arcade-goers in 1986 were playtesting The Lost Levels and didn't know it.

One more tell that you're on the arcade version: the Super Player's table. The NES game kept no permanent record of your greatness — VS. Super Mario Bros. keeps a top-ten board with initials and the world each run reached. Which brings us to this particular machine:

[Photo: The VS. Super Mario Bros. title screen running on the Nintendo UniSystem cabinet, control panel below]

***The real thing** — VS. Super Mario Bros. on the dedicated UniSystem. The cabinet → (https://www.orlandu.com/vs-unisystem.html)*

[Photo: VS. Super Mario Bros. Super Player's high score table, all ten entries initialed DK, all reaching world 8-4]

***The house board** — all ten slots initialed DK, all ten runs to World 8-4, 2,743,550 on top*

Every slot on this board is initialed DK, every run went the distance to World 8-4, and the top score stands at 2,743,550. On a version of Super Mario Bros. built specifically to stop that from happening. No visiting initials have cracked the list yet — the machine is on free play, so bring your A-game.

# Projects

Everything here gets worked on, not just displayed. The current bench queue, planned builds, and a trail of completed restorations.

## On the bench now
 In progress

An intermittent failure on cold boot. The interlock switch has been replaced and ruled out; a memory-protect switch is on order and next in line. Classic 90s Williams diagnosis: one suspect at a time.
 Ongoing

The primary E/F-series broadcast monitor has three open card slots waiting for the right input cards. See the wanted list (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html).

The deep technical write-up is finished — history, internals, the module system, a registry of documented frames and the market record. Read the monograph → (https://www.orlandu.com/ams-100-monograph.html)
 Out for service

### JVC X'Eye — full servicing

The Genesis/Sega CD combo unit is off at iFixRetro (@ifixretro (https://www.instagram.com/ifixretro/)) for a complete going-over. It'll come home better than new.

## Planned builds
 Planned

### WLED garage lighting

Addressable RGB throughout the arcade bay: WS2815 strip, ESP32 running WLED, a proper Mean Well supply, and aluminum channel so it looks built-in, not taped-on.
 Planned

### Arcade bay airflow

A room full of running CRTs makes real heat. A thermostat-controlled exhaust fan is the plan for keeping the tandem bay happy in summer.

## Completed
 Fixed

### Sony AMS-3 — volume pots cleaned

Two AMS-3s arrived untested, and they are monsters: 35 lbs apiece — a 14-inch PVM's worth of steel and heatsink for a *speaker* — and loud enough to hold their own in a room full of running CRTs. One has since moved on to another collector. The keeper had exactly one thing wrong with it, a scratchy volume pot, and a can of fader cleaner sorted it. See it next to an AMS-100 → (https://www.orlandu.com/ams-3-vs-ams-100.html)
 Completed

### Big Blue PSU rebuild

Full rebuild of the cabinet's switching supply, with voltages trimmed to spec. The foundation everything else in the cab depends on. Before and after → (https://www.orlandu.com/big-blue.html)
 Completed

### Indiana Jones board replacement

Rottendog main driver board and Fliptronics board fitted to the Williams widebody, alongside a full shop-out. The full work log → (https://www.orlandu.com/indiana-jones.html)
 Completed

### Big Blue side art installed

The decal hunt paid off — Capcom-logo side art is on the cabinet, finishing the look the PSU rebuild started. The full work log → (https://www.orlandu.com/big-blue.html)
 Completed

### Capcom Q-Sound amp repair

RCA jack reflow on a CPB-001A Q-Sound amplifier — small fix, big soundstage. The full work log → (https://www.orlandu.com/big-blue.html)
 Completed

### LMD fleet scan-mode setup

The LMD squadron configured for zero scan (with the 940W on Normal), trading a little edge clipping for the full-frame look.
 Completed

### BVM-20E1U calibration

Chased down a gain calibration quirk on the primary BVM — the kind of menu-diving only broadcast monitors ask of you.
 Completed

### PS2 MemCard Pro 2 setup

A PS2 slim running its library through FMCB/OPL from a MemCard Pro 2 — modern convenience, original hardware.

title: Speak Arcade & Broadcast: A Glossary
description: The words this site uses without stopping to explain them — JAMMA, CPO, candy cab, shop-out, NOS, RGB, 240p, SCART, BNC, BKM, TVL and the rest.
text:
Read Before Reading

# Speak Arcade & Broadcast

This site talks the way the hobby talks, which means it uses a lot of words without stopping to explain them. Here they are explained — the cabinet side first, then the glass. Nothing on this page is a secret; it is just the vocabulary nobody hands you at the door.
 The cabinetsThe glass

## The cabinets arcade and pinball

- **Upright**: The standing cabinet everyone pictures: monitor at eye level, controls at the waist, marquee over the top. Four of them live in the garage row.
- **Cocktail**: A table-height cabinet with the screen facing up through the glass, built for bars and pizza parlors where people sat down. The Red Tent (https://www.orlandu.com/red-tent.html) is Nintendo's two-screen version.
- **Candy cab**: The Japanese style of cabinet: molded plastic, sit-down height, pastel colors, and a monitor that usually rotates for vertical games. The pink Mini Cute (https://www.orlandu.com/mini-cute.html) is the smallest one Capcom made.
- **Widebody**: A cabinet built wider than standard — for a two-player control panel on an upright, or for a bigger playfield on a pinball machine. Mario Bros. (https://www.orlandu.com/mario-bros.html) is the one; Indiana Jones (https://www.orlandu.com/indiana-jones.html) is the other.
- **Dedicated**: A cabinet built by the manufacturer for one specific game, with that game's artwork and controls from the factory — as opposed to a conversion, where an operator swapped a new board and marquee into an old cabinet.
- **Marquee**: The backlit sign across the top of an upright naming the game. Original ones are printed on translucent plastic and are among the first things to crack, fade or go missing.
- **Topper**: On a pinball machine, the decoration mounted above the backbox. On a PlayChoice-10, a printed sticker on a metal stand that announced which game was new inside — nineteen of those are here (https://www.orlandu.com/signage.html#toppers).
- **Instruction card**: The printed card fixed beside the controls that told a player the rules and buttons. On Nintendo's VS. cabinets it changed with every board swap, which is why the unused ones (https://www.orlandu.com/signage.html#cards) are collected.
- **CPO control panel overlay**: The printed sheet laminated over the control panel, carrying the artwork and the button labels. The part hands wear through first, and one of the first things replaced on a restoration.
- **Side art**: The printed graphics on the sides of a cabinet. Originals are screen-printed or applied as large decals; reproductions exist for most popular games and are a normal part of a restoration.
- **JAMMA**: The standard connector and pinout the Japanese arcade industry agreed on in 1985, so one wiring harness could power and drive almost any game board. A JAMMA cabinet takes a JAMMA board; a pre-JAMMA cabinet, like the Nintendo uprights here, needs its own wiring or an adapter.
- **PCB the board**: The printed circuit board that *is* the game. Swap the board and the cabinet plays something else. Original boards are collected in their own right, some for absurd money.
- **Multi**: A single board that carries a whole library of games selectable from a menu, usually a flash-storage kit fitted to genuine period hardware. The Darksoft kits in Big Blue (https://www.orlandu.com/big-blue.html) (CPS-2) and the Mini Cute (https://www.orlandu.com/mini-cute.html) (CPS-1) are the ones here.
- **CPS-1 / CPS-2**: Capcom's arcade hardware of the late eighties and nineties — the CP System ran Street Fighter II and Final Fight; the CP System II ran the Alpha series, the Marvel fighters and Progear. Both take a JAMMA harness.
- **Suicide battery**: The battery on a CPS-2 board that keeps its encryption keys alive. When it dies, the board forgets how to run its own game — it "suicides." The reason a multi with no battery is worth having.
- **VS. System**: Nintendo's 1984 arcade platform built on NES-grade hardware, with games on swappable boards. It came as a single-screen UniSystem and a two-screen DualSystem; one of each (https://www.orlandu.com/vs-unisystem.html) is here (https://www.orlandu.com/red-tent.html).
- **PlayChoice-10**: Nintendo's later arcade system that held up to ten NES games on swappable cards and sold *time* rather than lives — a quarter bought a countdown, and you could hop between games while it ran.
- **Interchanger**: A switcher that lets one VS. cabinet hold two boards and choose between them without opening the door. The UniSystem (https://www.orlandu.com/vs-unisystem.html) runs one, so it plays both VS. Super Mario Bros. and VS. Duck Hunt.
- **Attract mode**: What a machine plays to itself when nobody is: the demo loop, the high score table, the title screen — designed to pull a passer-by across the room.
- **Free play**: The operator setting that removes the need for coins. Every machine here is on it, which is why the coin doors are decorative.
- **Shop-out**: Pinball's word for a full service: playfield stripped of every part, cleaned, rubbers and bulbs replaced, mechanisms rebuilt, reassembled. Not every machine needs one — one bought new from the factory never did.
- **Playfield**: The wooden surface under the glass where the ball lives, with all its ramps, targets and toys. The single most expensive thing on a pinball machine to replace.
- **Backglass / translite**: The illustrated panel in the backbox. A backglass is painted on glass; a translite is printed on plastic film behind clear glass. Originals fade, flake and crack, so good reproductions are prized.
- **DMD dot matrix display**: The orange dot display in the backbox of a nineties machine. A ColorDMD is a drop-in color replacement for it.
- **DCS**: Williams' Digital Compression System, the 1993 sound hardware that replaced tinny sample playback with something close to a film soundtrack. Indiana Jones (https://www.orlandu.com/indiana-jones.html) was in the first year of it.
- **Magna-slings**: Magnetic slingshots in place of the usual rubber ones, which grab the ball and throw it somewhere you did not plan for. Stern's Ghostbusters (https://www.orlandu.com/ghostbusters.html) Premium and LE have them, and everyone has an opinion.
- **HUO home use only**: A machine that was never on a commercial route — bought new and kept in a home from the first day. The most valuable four letters in a pinball listing.
- **On route**: The working life of a coin-op machine: placed in a bar or arcade by an operator, serviced on a schedule, and moved when the earnings dropped. Route wear is where most of the damage on a survivor comes from.
- **NOS new old stock**: Old parts or printed matter that were never used — still in the drawer, still on the backing paper. The instruction cards on the card wall (https://www.orlandu.com/signage.html#cards) are NOS; that is the whole point of them.
- **KLOV**: The Killer List of Videogames, now the Museum of the Game: the reference database of arcade games and the forum where much of this hobby lives. The handle orlandu81 has been there a long time.

## The glass monitors and signals

- **CRT**: Cathode ray tube: the glass display every one of these games was drawn for. An electron beam paints the picture line by line on phosphor, which is why pixel art looks right on one and slightly wrong on everything since.
- **Trinitron**: Sony's aperture-grille tube design, introduced in 1968 and used across its consumer televisions and professional monitors. Flatter vertically, brighter, and the reason the badge means something.
- **Aperture grille**: The fine vertical wires behind a Trinitron's screen that steer the beam to the right phosphor stripe, in place of the shadow mask other tubes use. It lets more light through; the trade is one or two faint horizontal damper wires you learn to stop seeing.
- **PVM / BVM / LMD**: Sony's professional families. **PVM**, Professional Video Monitor, the studio workhorse. **BVM**, Broadcast Video Monitor, the reference grade with hand-selected tubes and plug-in cards. **LMD**, the flat-panel generation that followed. The long version. (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-vs-bvm.html)
- **RGB**: Red, green and blue carried as three separate signals straight from the console's video chip, nothing blended on the way. The single biggest reason these monitors matter to games.
- **Composite**: The single yellow-plug video signal of the consumer era, with all the color information squeezed into one wire and smeared in the process. Not welcome on the monitors here.
- **Component**: Video split into three signals over three cables — luminance and two color-difference channels — the analog standard for DVD and early HD. What the LMD wall is fed.
- **240p**: The picture almost every classic console actually produces: 240 progressive lines, drawn every frame, at the 15 kHz scan rate of standard television. A CRT shows it with visible scanlines; a flat panel has to guess.
- **15 kHz**: The horizontal scan rate of standard-definition television and of nearly every arcade board and classic console. A monitor that locks to it will show them natively; one that does not needs a converter in the way.
- **Multiscan**: A monitor that locks to a range of scan rates rather than one — 15 kHz for a Super Nintendo, 31 kHz for 480p, higher for HD — on the same tube. The PVM-20L5 (https://www.orlandu.com/pvm-20l5-buying-guide.html) is the famous one.
- **Scanlines**: The dark gaps between the lines a 240p picture draws on a CRT. Not a defect: part of how the art was meant to look, and impossible to fake convincingly.
- **Scaler / line doubler**: A box that converts a 240p analog signal into something a flat panel accepts, adding processing and a frame or two of delay while it thinks. The signal chain here (https://www.orlandu.com/signal-chain.html) has none, on purpose.
- **SCART**: The big rectangular European connector that carries RGB video and stereo audio in one plug. The retro-console world speaks it; Sony's professional monitors do not, which is why the next entry exists.
- **BNC**: The twist-lock coaxial connector broadcast equipment uses, one per signal. A row of them on the back is the quickest tell that you are looking at a professional monitor. How to spot one. (https://www.orlandu.com/crt-field-guide.html)
- **SCART to 4 BNC breakout**: The cable that joins the two worlds: SCART on one end, four BNCs — red, green, blue and sync — on the other, with an audio pair broken out beside them.
- **Sync**: The timing signal that tells the monitor where each line and frame begins. It can ride on its own wire, on the green channel, or inside a composite signal; professional Sony monitors are far less fussy about which than folklore says.
- **Switcher**: A box with many inputs and one or two outputs so several consoles can share a monitor. An auto-switcher picks whichever console is powered on, which is what makes a large collection playable rather than just owned.
- **Distribution amplifier**: A box that takes one signal in and sends an identical, re-driven copy to many outputs — unlike a passive splitter, which halves the signal every time it divides. Behind the LMD wall (https://www.orlandu.com/monitors.html).
- **Loop-through**: A second connector beside an input that passes the same signal out again, so monitors can be daisy-chained. The last one in the chain gets a termination switch set to 75 ohms.
- **BKM card**: Sony's plug-in input boards for the BVM and late PVM chassis. Each card teaches the monitor another signal format, so on these monitors the slots *are* the inputs. Several are on the wanted list (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html).
- **TVL TV lines**: The resolution figure Sony quoted for its tubes: how many alternating vertical lines the screen can resolve across a width equal to its height. A production PVM runs around 600 to 800; a BVM, around 1000.
- **SMPTE-C**: The broadcast color standard for phosphors in North America. A monitor built to it shows colors where the mastering engineer put them, which a store-bought set never promised.
- **Geometry / convergence**: Whether straight lines are straight and evenly spaced across the screen, and whether the red, green and blue beams land on the same spot. The first things to check on any tube, and the expensive ones to fix.
- **Degauss**: The coil that fires on power-up to clear stray magnetism from the shadow mask or grille. If the corners of a screen have gone pink or green, it has usually been a while.
- **Burn-in**: The ghost of an image a tube displayed for too long, worn permanently into the phosphor. Arcade monitors that spent years in attract mode often carry it; the ones here that came out clean are remarked on for a reason.
- **Zero scan / underscan**: Showing the entire picture inside the screen edge instead of pushing the outer few percent past it the way a television does. A professional monitor lets you choose.
- **ISR**: Sony's serial remote control system for professional monitors: one controller, a daisy-chained cable, and a whole wall of monitors taking the same commands. The reason a BVM has a remote port beside its inputs.
- **Audio monitor**: A small self-powered speaker built to sit in a rack and let an engineer hear whether the sound is there and clean. Sony's AMS-100 units ride on top of the monitors here; the monograph (https://www.orlandu.com/ams-100-monograph.html) is about them.
- **RGB mod**: A board fitted inside a console that never officially output RGB — the NES above all — to make it do so. The NESRGB in the top loader on the consoles page (https://www.orlandu.com/consoles.html) is one.

Missing a word? Email orlandusarcade@gmail.com and it will get an entry. Several of the monitor terms above are also explained, with pictures, in Trinitron Fleet, Vol. 1 (https://www.orlandu.com/trinitron-fleet-vol1.html).

Player 2 Wanted

# For Sale

The collection consolidates over time — duplicates and departures get listed so they can go to someone who'll use them. Sales run through eBay with years of seller history behind them.

## Currently listed

[Photo: Baseball Stars PlayChoice-10 game board, component side above and solder side below]

 On eBay · $89.99 PlayChoice-10 game board

### Baseball Stars

The NES baseball game people still play. It arrived in 1989, late enough that far fewer boards shipped than the mid-decade titles. Tested and working, fully original: every Nintendo marking reads B9, with no rework anywhere. Needs a PlayChoice-10 motherboard — it won’t run in an NES.

[Photo: Captain Skyhawk PlayChoice-10 game board, component side above and solder side below]

 On eBay · $169.99 PlayChoice-10 game board

### Captain Skyhawk

One of only two PlayChoice-10 titles built on the “I” type board — Solar Jetman is the other, and both are where a set build stalls. Original ROMs, stickers unlifted, every Nintendo marking reading YW. Needs a PlayChoice-10 motherboard — it won’t run in an NES.

[Photo: Contra PlayChoice-10 game board, component side above and solder side below]

 On eBay · $159.99 PlayChoice-10 game board

### Contra

The most in-demand title on the platform, then and now. An early example: 1987 copyrights on both the Nintendo silkscreen and the Konami label, all three ROMs in their factory sockets and marked CT. Needs a PlayChoice-10 motherboard — it won’t run in an NES.

 More on eBay

### Vintage gaming & electronics

Collectibles, arcade hardware, and rare electronics get listed regularly — 100% positive feedback across 1,400+ ratings, 500+ items sold.

Prices shown are eBay asking prices, with eBay's fees baked in. Buying direct? Email orlandusarcade@gmail.com for better pricing.

Selling isn't the only direction — the arcade is buying, too. The hunt list (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html) names exactly what it's after, and fair prices are paid.

Player One

# About Orlandu's Arcade

[Photo: The Orlandu's Arcade mascot — a wandering warrior with a staff and an arcade cabinet on his back]

Orlandu's Arcade is a private arcade and working collection in Orange County, California, spread across two rooms: the garage arcade, where the upright cabinets, the pinball row, and the broadcast monitor racks live, and the game room inside the house, home to the candy cab, the cocktail, and the big PVMs. Between them runs a fleet of Sony professional monitors that most video engineers would recognize before most gamers would.

The philosophy here is simple: everything runs. Cabinets get their power supplies rebuilt, pinball machines get their mechs restored, monitors get calibrated the way Sony intended. This isn't a museum behind glass — it's a garage where the CRTs are warm and the high-score initials still get entered.

The name comes from the handle "orlandu81," a long-standing identity across the KLOV / Museum of the Game forums, Arcade-Projects, and eBay. The mascot — a wandering warrior hauling an arcade cabinet on his back — pretty much sums up the lifestyle.

Alongside the collecting there's an active trade in vintage gaming collectibles, arcade hardware, and rare electronics — what's for sale now (https://www.orlandu.com/forsale.html), and what the arcade is hunting (https://www.orlandu.com/wanted.html).

## Inside the game room one full turn

***A 33-second spin** — the framed PCB wall, Super Mario Bros. on the PVMs, the fiber-optic Kay·Bee World of Nintendo sign, and the Mini Cute and Red Tent holding their corners*

title: Use orlandu.com From Your AI Assistant
description: An MCP server, llms.txt, a full-text file and three open datasets let Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any agent search the arcade's site, read its pages and query its Sony monitor specs.
text:
For AI Agents

# Ask Your Assistant About the Arcade

Everything on this site is readable by an AI assistant, and now callable by one. An MCP server lets Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Claude Code or any agent that speaks the protocol search the site, read a page in full and query the open datasets — no key, no account, no scraping.

## Three ways in

- **llms.txt** — a one-page index of the site for agents: https://www.orlandu.com/llms.txt (https://www.orlandu.com/llms.txt)
- **llms-full.txt** — the whole site's text in one Markdown file, about 74,000 words, for an agent that wants to read everything at once: https://www.orlandu.com/llms-full.txt (https://www.orlandu.com/llms-full.txt)
- **The MCP server** — tools an agent can call: https://www.orlandu.com/api/mcp

## The MCP server

Endpoint https://www.orlandu.com/api/mcp — Streamable HTTP transport, read-only, no authentication. Six tools:

- search_orlandu — full-text search over every page, card, glossary term and gallery caption
- read_orlandu_page — one page as Markdown
- list_orlandu_pages — every page with its description
- sony_monitor_specs — the fleet spec table, filterable by model
- playchoice_10_library — the fifty-two PlayChoice-10 games, each with its board photo
- console_video_out — how each console reaches the glass

It answers from the published pages only, and it is rebuilt with every update to the site.

## Connect it

Wherever your assistant takes a remote MCP server, give it the URL above. In Claude Code it is one line:

```
claude mcp add --transport http orlandu https://www.orlandu.com/api/mcp
```

In Cursor, add it to mcp.json:

```
{ "mcpServers": { "orlandu": { "url": "https://www.orlandu.com/api/mcp" } } }
```

In Claude it goes in as a custom connector with that URL; ChatGPT and most other assistants that accept a remote MCP server take the same URL. Then ask: *"Which Sony monitors at Orlandu's Arcade take BKM cards, and which cards are fitted?"* · *"What does the PVM-20L5 buying guide say about shipping?"* · *"Read the PVM vs. BVM piece and tell me which one I want for a Super Nintendo."*

## The datasets

Three tables from the site as open data, CC BY 4.0 — use them, credit Orlandu's Arcade.

| Dataset | What's in it | Files |
|---|---|---|
| Sony monitor specs | Eight models, thirteen columns: display, size, resolution, formats, inputs, option slots, weight, era — the fleet table (https://www.orlandu.com/monitors.html#specs) | JSON (https://www.orlandu.com/data/sony-monitor-specs.json) · CSV (https://www.orlandu.com/data/sony-monitor-specs.csv) |
| PlayChoice-10 library | The fifty-two games Nintendo released, each with a photo of its original board — the cart wall (https://www.orlandu.com/playchoice-10.html) | JSON (https://www.orlandu.com/data/playchoice-10-library.json) · CSV (https://www.orlandu.com/data/playchoice-10-library.csv) |
| Console video out | Nine consoles: the modification, the video output, the chain to the monitor — the console table (https://www.orlandu.com/consoles.html#mods) | JSON (https://www.orlandu.com/data/console-video-out.json) · CSV (https://www.orlandu.com/data/console-video-out.csv) |

The photos the datasets link to stay © Orlandu's Arcade.

## The rules

Read-only, free, and rate-limited only by courtesy: one assistant reading a few pages is the use this was built for; a crawler should take llms-full.txt (https://www.orlandu.com/llms-full.txt) instead. The text and photography are © Orlandu's Arcade, and quoting with attribution is welcome. The arcade is a private collection in a home, not a venue — and the server will tell your assistant the same.
